en: The *Adhikaraṇavastu* (Adhik-v 59): Regarding the matters for settling legal disputes (*adhikaraṇaśamathavastu*), the summary verse (*uddāna*) states: "Quarrel, dispute, the legal dispute, its root, and that which is wholesome."
There may be a dispute that is not a formal legal case; with how many [factors] should one settle such a dispute?
One should settle a dispute face-to-face by means of taking up voting tickets;
and one should settle a lack of instruction face-to-face by means of mindfulness and the verdict of those no longer deluded.

In the same way, there is the *tatsvabhāvaiṣīya* (decision by the nature of the case), as well as the *tṛṇaprastāraka* (covering over with grass), and likewise the settlement of legal matters (*kṛtyādhikaraṇa*) by the entire Saṃgha.
"It must be thoroughly stilled," so it was proclaimed by the Great Seer.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Kapilavastu in the Nyagrodha Grove; there, King Śuddhodana listened to the Buddha’s discourses.
When the Blessed One had established the Śākyas in the [Noble] Truths, they would approach the Blessed One for a vision three times;
the Blessed One frequently taught them the Dharma.
It was the custom of King Śuddhodana, surrounded by the Śākya host, to approach the Blessed One for a vision three times.
Then, at another time, the Blessed One sat before an assembly of many hundreds and taught the Dharma like pure, unalloyed honey;
and the assembly of many hundreds listened to the most sweet Dharma from the presence of the Blessed One with unmoving faculties.
King Śuddhodana, accompanied by great royal splendor and great royal majesty, surrounded by the Śākya host, approached the Blessed One in order to hear the Dharma;
having heard the Dharma, he departed.
The Buddha’s teaching is addressed to women as well.
Queen Mahāprajāpatī asked King Śuddhodana to grant permission for the Śākya women to hear the Dharma.

Then Mahānāman the Śākya, having heard the Dharma and conceived faith in the presence of the Blessed One, went to his own home and said: "O Buddha! O Dharma! O Saṅgha! The appearance of the Buddha has borne fruit for us!"
Mahānāman’s chief queen said:
"Noble son, what is this? He replied:
"Today, before an assembly of many hundreds, the Blessed One has taught such a Dharma that, having heard it, many hundreds of thousands of living beings have attained a great distinction.
She said: "Noble son, what you say—that the appearance of a Buddha is fruitful for us—is indeed true."
"The arising of a Buddha is indeed fruitful for you, but not for us.
Why is that?
Because the Blessed One, the Buddha, has appeared in the world for the sake of men, not for women."
He said: "O noble lady, do not speak thus; the Blessed One is compassionate and seeks the welfare of all sentient beings."
"You too should go and listen to the Dharma from the presence of the Blessed One.
She said:
"The King, surrounded by the Śākya host, approaches the Blessed One three times for an audience;
we would be ashamed to hear the Dharma in the presence of the King and before his face."
"Therefore, if Your Majesty would go once every day at the start of the forenoon, we too might hear the Dharma from the presence of the Blessed One in the afternoon.
Mahānāman the Śākya reflected: "I shall go;
I will awaken the King."
Again he reflected:
"It is distressing that the King is being petitioned for the sake of his own wives;
Mahāprajāpatī is highly esteemed by the King."
"Whatever she considers ought to be heard or done, I shall report this matter to her. He then approached Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
Having approached, he reported this matter to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī;
she said:
"So be it;
I shall awaken the King.
Then the householder Mahānāman went home and informed the Śākyāyanīs.
Then those Śākyāyanīs and others approached Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī;
having approached her, they said this to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī: "Gautamī, you should know that..."
"We have heard, Blessed One, that you teach the Dharma most sweetly before an assembly of many hundreds, like pure honey free from bees,
and that this assembly of many hundreds listens to the most sweet Dharma from the presence of the Blessed One with unmoving faculties.
Therefore, we too wish to hear the Dharma from the presence of the Blessed One."
"Request the Lord on our behalf so that the Lord may approach the Blessed One in the forenoon and we may do so in the afternoon.
She said, "Sisters,
you have conceived an excellent thought."
"Wait a moment while I look upon King Śuddhodana.
Then Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī approached King Śuddhodana;
having approached him, she spoke thus to King Śuddhodana.
"Indeed, Your Majesty, you should know this: I have heard that the Blessed One, seated before an assembly of many hundreds, teaches the Dharma most sweetly, like pure honey free from bees;
and the assembly of many hundreds listens to the Dharma from the presence of the Blessed One with unmoving faculties."
The Śākya nuns have also heard this:
they desire to hear the Dharma.
Therefore, Your Majesty, it would be fitting for you to approach the presence of the Blessed One in the forenoon.

I too shall take the Śākya women and approach the Blessed One in the afternoon; for what reason? Because they are occupied with household chores in the forenoon and do not find the opportunity to approach the Blessed One.

It was the custom of King Śuddhodana that whenever Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī gave an order, he would remain with his body upright and the king would not sit down until Mahāprajāpatī’s command had been carried out;
bowing his head, he said, "Gautamī," and so on.
"Let it be so for him.
(Adhik-v 62) Examples of female vanity and the story of the maidservant Rohikā:
Then Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, surrounded by five hundred Śākya women, went to the Nyagrodha Grove to hear the Dharma from the presence of the Blessed One.
Meanwhile, Mahāprajāpatī Śākyā went along with her, adorned with all her ornaments;
being possessed of beauty and youth and decked out in every ornament, she began to cast glances that could stir the hearts of those who had not yet overcome passion.
She was seen by the Venerable Ānanda, who said to her: "Sister,"
You are already naturally beautiful, lovely, and pleasing to behold;
how much more so when adorned with all your ornaments!
It was not well done of you that you came having put on these ornaments.
"These great-souled ones are not all free from passion";
having been addressed thus, her heart overcome with shame, she cast down her face, withdrew to a secluded spot, removed that ornament, and remained there lost in thought.
She had a maidservant named Rohakā;
she had come together with her, desiring to hear the Dharma.
She was called by her and addressed as follows:
“Go, Rohikā, leave this ornament here and return.
She, moving with a swift gait, left it in the house and returned.
Then Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, together with her retinue of five hundred, bowed her head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
The Blessed One began to teach the Dharma;
while that Dharma was being taught, a certain Śākya maiden repeatedly looked at a pearl necklace hanging from her ear and touched it with her hand.
Then the Blessed One began to teach the Dharma connected with impermanence;
nevertheless, she did not remain [attentive], but continued to gaze at the pearl necklace.
The chief queen of Mahānāman saw that Śākyan maiden gazing again and again at the pearl necklace fastened upon her ear;
and having seen her, this thought occurred to her:
"Why is this poor woman so excessively attached to this pearl necklace, even while these conditioned phenomena, which are thus impermanent, are being taught?"
Thinking, "If she were to see my pearl necklace, all her intoxication would vanish," he addressed his maidservant Rohikā:
"Go, bring my pearl necklace quickly.
To her, whose mind was captivated by hearing the Dharma, this thought occurred:
"Alas, what a tragedy! While such a Dharma was being taught, my mistress gave the command; thus an obstacle to the Dharma has arisen.
'In every way, the state of servitude is miserable'—realizing this, they were struck by pain and despondency."
And he spoke this verse:
"Fie on this state of servitude, so full of suffering and dependent on another! Fie on my life, obtained through the karma performed in the past! (Adhik-v 63)
For today I do not obtain even a glimpse of the Victor’s face, nor do I hear a single word of that Sugata’s stainless Dharma.
Thus it was. Then this thought occurred to the Blessed One:
"This girl Rohikā has performed meritorious services under previous Buddhas, yet her lifespan is short;
she must be delivered from the prison of saṃsāra. Having understood this, he wrote a verse on birch bark by means of his supernormal power and gave it to her.
Knowing indeed that what has arisen must perish,
O auspicious lady, you should apply yourself with effort to what is auspicious and listen to my speech.
Thus it was said; then the maiden Rohikā, thrilled, satisfied, and filled with joy and gladness, spoke this verse:
"With a mind directed solely toward the Buddha as its object, those who have set out on the path do not perish, even after hundreds of eons."
Having obtained the necessary conditions and the right time, the actions of embodied beings indeed bear fruit.
Thus it was: the causal conditions for a short lifespan had been met;
she was deprived of life by a young cow;
having developed a mind of serene faith toward the Blessed One, she passed away.
The Story of Muktikā,
Daughter of the King of Siṃhala,
and the Portrait of the Buddha
She was conceived in the womb of the chief queen of the King of Siṃhala on the island of Siṃhala; on the very day she took rebirth, a rain of pearls fell.
The king summoned the fortune-tellers and questioned them.
They said: "Your Majesty, it is due to the power of this being who has been conceived in the womb of the queen.
Thereupon, he was attended to with cooling requisites when it was cold and with warming requisites prescribed by physicians when it was hot.
With foods that were not excessively bitter, not excessively sour, not excessively salty, not excessively sweet, not excessively pungent,

and not excessively astringent— foods devoid of bitterness, acidity, saltiness, sweetness, pungency, and astringency— the woman, her body adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces like an apsaras wandering in the Nandana grove, did not descend from couch to couch or seat to seat, but remained on the lower level.
And she did not hear any unpleasant sound whatsoever until the fetus was fully matured;
after the lapse of eight or nine months, she gave birth,
and sons were born who were handsome, beautiful, and pleasing to behold.
On the very day she was born, a rain of pearls fell.
The king reflected:
"If this rain of pearls has fallen by the power of the girl, let these pearls belong to her alone."
He had them presented to her alone;
then, after performing the birth festival in detail for three weeks— twenty-one days— he established a name for her.
"What shall be the name of this girl?
the ministers asked.
They replied, "Since a rain of pearls has fallen through the power of her merit, therefore let the name of this girl be 'Muktā' (Pearl)."
The name Muktā was established for her; the girl Muktā was entrusted to eight nurses: two to serve as her shoulder-nurses, and so forth.
by two nurses who provided milk, by two nurses who cleaned him, and by two nurses who played with him;

She was raised and nurtured by eight nurses with milk, curd, fresh butter, ghee, the cream of ghee, and other various excellent provisions most refined; she grew quickly like a lotus in a pond. When she had become a young woman, she became exceedingly well-regarded by the king and his household for her conduct and deportment, which were in perfect accordance with her own family lineage.

Then, at another time, some merchants from Śrāvastī set out upon the great ocean in a sea-going vessel to fetch wealth. Having successfully completed their voyage, they were driven by the wind and arrived at the island of Siṃhala.
There, having unloaded their merchandise, they settled down not far from the royal palace.

At the time of dawn, as they were reciting in detail the Udānas, the Pārāyaṇas, the Satyadṛśas, the Verses of the Elders, the Verses of the Elder Nuns, the Verses on the Śailas, the Verses of the Sages, and the Sections on Meaning, she heard them from her window while still in her chamber;
thereupon, she informed the king: "Your Majesty," she said.
"Merchants who have arrived from the Middle Country are singing beautifully";
the king gave this command to his ministers: "Sirs, let the singers be summoned."
They were summoned; Muktikā said: "Sirs, sing!"
"We hear about what kind of music there is in the Middle Country;
they replied, 'Your Majesty,
we are not musicians.'"
"We are merchants from Śrāvastī who have come here by the force of the wind; at the break of dawn last night, we recited the words of the Buddha.
Upon hearing this sound of "Buddha," a term she had never heard before, all of Muktikā’s pores bristled with joy.
Filled with curiosity, she asked:
"Sirs, who is this one called Buddha?
They began to describe the greatness of the Buddha in detail: "O Queen," they said, [he is...]
A prince was born among the Śākyas on the side of the Himalayas, on the bank of the river Bhāgīrathī, not far from the hermitage of the seer Kapila;
he was prophesied by Brahmins who were skilled in signs and interpretation.
If he remains a householder and dwells at home, he will become a universal monarch, a conqueror of the four quarters, righteous and a king of Dharma, endowed with the seven jewels.
These will be his seven such jewels, namely: the wheel-jewel, the elephant-jewel, the horse-jewel, the gem-jewel, the woman-jewel, the householder-jewel, and the counselor-jewel as the seventh.
He will have a full thousand sons—heroes, warriors, handsome in form and limb, crushers of enemy armies;

he will dwell having conquered this entire great earth, bounded by the ocean, without exception, free from thorns, free from calamities, by means of righteousness alone, without punishment or weapons, and with impartiality.

If, however, he shaves off his hair and beard, puts on saffron robes, and out of perfect faith goes forth from the home to the homeless life, he will become a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha.
"His fame resounds throughout the world; he alone is called 'Buddha'. Thus spoke Muktikā.
"When it is time for your departure, you shall inform me";
they replied,
"So be it, O Queen."
"We shall announce it";
meanwhile, the time and place for their departure arrived;
by them, from Muktikā—
It was reported; she wrote a letter to the Blessed One:
"O you who are honored by asuras, gods, and humans, I have gone forth out of fear of birth, disease, and danger."
O Lord, whose vast fame and renown have spread abroad, O Sage, grant me an incomparable portion of the nectar of immortality.
Thus it was said; then those merchants, taking that letter, arrived in Śrāvastī by stages;
having dispelled the fatigue of the road, they approached the Blessed One, prostrated with their heads at the Blessed One’s feet, and sat down to one side.
The merchants of Śrāvastī said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, this letter was sent by the daughter of King Siṃhala of Siṃhaladvīpa to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One, knowing that the time for Muktikā’s conversion had come, took it up himself and read it."
Having had it read aloud, he said:
"When you have to go again, you shall inform me.
"So be it, Venerable Sir," those merchants replied, bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, and departed from his presence.
Then, having sold their merchandise and taken goods in exchange, they approached the Blessed One and said:
"Blessed One, we are about to set out; please give us your command—what words of release should we speak?"
The Blessed One said:
"Bring a well-prepared cloth and some painters.
They brought the cloth, and the painters were summoned.
The Blessed One said:
"Have an image of the Tathāgata painted on a cloth"; the painters then began their work.
To paint an image of the Buddha;
the painters were unable to produce a likeness of the Tathāgata, which is brought forth by hundreds of manifold merits.
The Blessed One said:
"Bring forth the cloth; I shall emit light.
By them, the cloth was brought forth.
The Blessed One emitted light;
it was filled by painters with various colors.
Then, beneath the image, the Blessed One [taught] the three goings for refuge, the five precepts, the twelvefold dependent origination in both forward and reverse order, and the noble eightfold path.
Recite the two verses above: "Go forth, apply yourselves to the teaching of the Buddha;
shake off the army of Death as an elephant shakes down a reed-thicket."
For whoever shall practice vigilantly in this Dharma and Vinaya,
having abandoned the cycle of birth, will make an end of suffering.
Thus it was said; and a letter was written to the King of Siṃhala.
I have dispatched a gift inscribed upon a cloth-painting of Muktikā.
You, having assembled the multitude of people dwelling on the island of Siṃhala in a spacious region of the earth, should honor this [gift] with great ceremony.
The cloth must be opened; and those merchants were instructed:
"If Muktikā asks, 'What is this?', you should say, 'This is the form-body (rūpakāya) of that Blessed One.'"
If he asks, "What is this below? What is this?", one should say:
"These are the three goings for refuge, the five precepts of training, dependent origination in direct and reverse order, and the proceeding and ceasing of the world."
"This is his realization: the noble eightfold path.
If he asks, "What is this above this?", you should say: "Encourage him!"
"Having taken up the precepts for going for refuge and having contemplated this twelvefold dependent origination in its forward and reverse order, he exerts vigor;
having attained the path to the realization of the deathless, he is liberated from all suffering.
"So be it, Venerable Sir," those merchants replied to the Blessed One and departed from his presence.

Then, having performed the auspicious rites and ceremonies for success, they took with them the merchandise intended for the island of Siṃhala and, traveling by stages, arrived at the island of Siṃhala;
having dispelled the fatigue of the journey, they approached the presence of the king.
Having prostrated at his feet, they presented the letter;
the king read the letter, and having read it,
he had that city cleared of stones, pebbles, and gravel, and sprinkled with sandalwood water.
With its flags and banners raised, its bundles of silk ribbons and garlands draped about, its fragrant incense burners set out, and strewn with various flowers,
the multitude of people dwelling in Siṃhala Island assembled. Then, having prepared a lion-throne made of the four jewels in the center of the city with great honor, the cloth was unveiled.

A great multitude of people raised a loud cry, "Homage to the Buddha! Homage to the Buddha! Then Princess Muktikā, her heart overcome by intense faith, her hair standing on end and her eyes clouded with tears, fell at their feet and asked those merchants, "Sirs, what is this?"
They began to explain:
"This is the physical body (rūpakāya) of that Blessed One;
what is this below?"
These are the three goings for refuge and the five precepts;
this is dependent origination in its forward and reverse order, as well as the proceeding and the cessation of the world;
this is the attainment of the deathless, the Noble Eightfold Path.
What follows this?
It is: having been encouraged and having taken up the precepts for going for refuge, one contemplates this twelvefold dependent origination in its forward and reverse order and exerts vigor.
"Having attained the path that leads to the realization of the Deathless, one is liberated from all suffering.

Thereupon, Muktikā began to contemplate the twelve-linked dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) in both forward and reverse order; however, before she had completed three full cycles, she shattered the mountain of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which rose up with its twenty peaks, by means of the mass of her knowledge, and realized the fruit of stream-entry (*srotaāpattiphala*).
Having seen the truths, she spoke this verse: "While standing at a distance, my eye of wisdom has been purified by the Buddha;
homage to that excellent physician whose medical treatment is such as this!"
Though standing afar, the Buddha has extracted the thorn of [wrong] views;
homage to that excellent physician who removes the thorn of views!
Having spoken this verse, he said to those merchants: "Sirs, when you go, you will find it agreeable.
Then, having disposed of their merchandise and taken goods in exchange, they approached Muktikā.
"O Queen, we have set out;
please command us what must be done by us. She replied:

"In my name, the feet of the Blessed One should be saluted with the head, and he should be asked whether he has little affliction, little illness, ease of movement, vigor, strength, comfort, blamelessness, and a state of well-being; and he should be addressed in this way:"

"Venerable sir, whatever was to be done by the spiritual friend Kalyāṇamitra has been accomplished by the Blessed One; having relied upon the Blessed One as my spiritual friend, I have been pulled out from the realms of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts, and established among gods and humans."
Samsara has been brought to its end; the oceans of blood and tears have been dried up;
the mountains of bones have been crossed.
Having shattered with a multitude of knowledges the mountain of the view of a self-identity accumulated since beginningless time, I have realized the fruit of stream-entry.
I have transcended, O Venerable One; I have transcended.
I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha of monks.
"Accept her as a laywoman from this day forward for as long as life lasts, one who has gone for refuge and is full of faith.
And "Take these three measures of pearls: one for the Buddha, one for the Dharma, and one for the Saṅgha.
Then those merchants, having taken their merchandise and the message, set out.
Having reached Śrāvastī by stages,
they dispelled their fatigue from the road and approached the presence of the Blessed One.
Prostrating at his feet and reporting everything exactly as he had instructed, they said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, these three measures of pearls have been sent by Muktikā—
one for the Buddha, one for the Dharma, and one for the Saṅgha.
Then the Venerable Ānanda asked the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, where has the gift arrived?
The Blessed One said:
"Ānanda, did you not see the Śākya woman Mahānāman’s maidservant named Rohikā, who departed after hearing the Dharma from me?"
"And on the way back, was she deprived of life by a cow with a young calf?
"I saw her, Venerable Sir; having developed a mind of serene faith toward me, she passed away."
On the island of Siṃhala, she became the daughter of the King of Siṃhala, named Muktikā;
having seen the Truths, she sent this gift.
Therefore, whoever is the Buddha's portion, let him apply it as an ointment in the fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭī).
"Whatever belongs to the Dharma is for those persons who uphold the Dharma;
whatever belongs to the Saṅgha, let the entire Saṅgha share that, O monks.
Having thus spoken, the monks, having conceived doubts, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the cutter of all doubts:
"Venerable sir, what karma did Muktikā perform by which she became a slave;
what karma did she perform by which she was reborn into a wealthy royal family; and how was the vision of the Truth attained?"
Thus it was said; the Blessed One replied:

"Monks, these actions were performed and accumulated by Muktikā herself; their conditions have been met, their causal factors have ripened, they have arrived like a surging flood, and they are inevitable. Who else shall experience the results of the actions performed and accumulated by Muktikā?"

“Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element, nor in the fire element, nor even in the wind element; rather, it is within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases that performed actions— whether wholesome or unwholesome— ripen.”
Actions do not perish even in hundreds of eons;
having encountered the necessary conditions and the right time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings.

The Story of the Wife of the Guild-Leader (Concerning a Previous Life of Muktikā). Monks, in the past, in this very Fortunate Eon, when the lifespan of beings was twenty thousand years, a Teacher named Kāśyapa appeared in the world, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata.
The Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed Charioteer of men to be tamed, the Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One—
having completed the entire work of a Buddha, passed away into the realm of Nirvana without remainder at Vārāṇasī, like a fire when its fuel is exhausted.
King Kṛkī had a pyre constructed for him using all kinds of fragrant wood and cremated him with great honor.
That pyre was extinguished with milk.
Having placed those bones in a golden urn, he erected a stūpa made of the four jewels at the crossroads, measuring one yojana in circumference and half a yojana in height, and held a grand festival.

And having been established in Vārāṇasī, there was a certain merchant who was very wealthy, possessed of great enjoyments, with extensive and vast property, accumulated wealth like that of Vaiśravaṇa, and rivaling the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa;
he brought home a wife from a family of equal status.
He played, took pleasure, and amused himself with her;
yet as he was playing, taking pleasure, and amusing himself, neither a son nor a daughter was born to him.
Placing his cheek in his hand, he remained lost in thought:
"My house is filled with manifold wealth,
yet I have neither son nor daughter;
upon my passing, because I am childless, my entire estate will become subject to the king."
He was told by ascetics, brahmins, friends, relatives, kinsmen, and diviners:
"Perform worship of the deities;
a son will be born to you."
Being childless and longing for a son, he made supplications to Śiva, Varuṇa, Kubera, Śakra, Brahmā, and other specific deities;

that is to say, he supplicated the deities of gardens, the deities of forests, the deities of crossroads, the deities of junctions, the deities who receive offerings, as well as innate deities, co-religious deities, and even those deities who are constantly attached to him.
Furthermore, there is this common saying in the world: "Sons and daughters are born as a result of supplication."
But that is not so;
if it were otherwise, every single person would have a thousand sons, just like a universal monarch (cakravartin).
Rather, sons and daughters are born through the coming together of three conditions.
Of which three? The mother and father are in love and have come together; the mother is healthy and in her fertile period; and a gandharva is present.
Through the presence of these three conditions, sons and daughters are born;
however, because he did not perform the karma conducive to having a son,
he has neither a son nor a daughter.
Eventually, he fell ill;
he was attended with medicines consisting of roots, stalks, leaves, flowers, and fruits,
yet that disease did not subside.
Then his wife reflected:
"My home is accumulated with much wealth, yet I have neither son nor daughter."
"And this master of mine will pass away;
therefore, if he does not now take provisions for the journey to the next world, then all this collection of wealth, being childless, will fall under the jurisdiction of the king.
She had a pearl necklace worth a hundred thousand [pieces] fastened to her ear.
Having performed an offering to the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa with perfumes, garlands, and ointments, she placed it upon that stūpa;
and with intense faith, prostrating at his feet, she made this aspiration:

"By this root of merit, by this production of the thought of awakening, and by this renunciation of things to be given, may I be born into a wealthy and great family; may I become a possessor of such qualities as these; and may I please, and never displease, such a Teacher as this. What do you think, monks?
She who was the merchant’s wife at that time and on that occasion was none other than this Muktikā;
it was because she made offerings at the stūpa of the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa and made a formal aspiration that [this result occurred].

Through the ripening of her karma, she was born into a wealthy family, and during this life a rain of pearls fell upon her; having conceived faith in my teaching, she shattered the mountain of the view of a self-identity— which rises with its twenty peaks— by means of the mass of knowledge, and realized the fruit of stream-entry.
Furthermore, she became the wife of a merchant who possessed vast wealth.
There, intoxicated by the pride of her power, she addressed every person she encountered with the word "slave.
As the ripening of that karma, she herself became a slave.
"Thus, monks, the ripening of entirely black actions is entirely black; the ripening of entirely white actions is entirely white; and the ripening of mixed actions is mixed.
Therefore, monks, having abandoned entirely black actions as well as mixed ones, you should apply yourselves solely to entirely white actions. In this way, monks, you should train yourselves."
Regarding the four classes of disputes, it was said by the Blessed One:
"That which is the portion of the Dharma belongs to those persons who are preachers of the Dharma."
In that regard, the Sūtrāntikas say:
"We uphold the entire sūtra of the Blessed One; we are the upholders of the Dharma."
"This gain belongs to us," they said.
The holders of the Vinaya replied,
"We are the guardians of the Blessed One's inner treasury."
"We uphold the entire Vinaya; we are upholders of the Dharma;
this gain has accrued to us."
The holders of the Mātṛkā say:
"We uphold the specific characteristics and the general characteristics of both the Sūtra and the Vinaya;
we are the upholders of the Dharma."
"This gain belongs to us," they said;
thereupon, a quarrel, a scuffle, a conflict, and a dispute arose among those who were masters of the Sūtras, masters of the Vinaya, and masters of the Mātṛkās.
Then the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"Monks, let there be no quarreling, no brawling, no strife, and no dispute.
Monks, there are these four legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*). Which four?"
The legal question of dispute, the legal question of censure, the legal question of offense, and the legal question of business.
What is the legal issue of dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*)?

It is that which is the Sangha’s discordant speech, contention, opposing speech, lack of harmony, lack of mutual delight, and state of division; based upon that, whatever quarreling, brawling, strife, and dispute there is—this is called [the legal issue of dispute].
What is the legal issue of non-admonition (*anavavādādhikaraṇa*)?

That which is the Sangha’s lack of instruction, non-instruction, and non-establishment of instruction—based upon that, whatever quarrel, strife, contention, or dispute arises—is called a legal issue concerning non-instruction (*anavavādādhikaraṇa*).
What is the legal issue concerning offenses (*āpattyadhikaraṇa*)?
The five types of offenses are called the aggregate of offenses (*āpattiskandha*).
Which five?
Pārājikas, saṃghāvaśeṣas, pāyattikas, pratideśanīyas, and duṣkṛtas.
Based on these, whatever quarrel, strife, contention, or dispute arises—this is called a legal issue concerning offenses (*āpattyadhikaraṇa*).
What is the legal issue concerning duties (*kṛtyādhikaraṇa*)?

It refers to whatever quarreling, strife, contention, and dispute arises based upon a formal act of the Saṃgha consisting of a motion (*jñapti*), or a motion followed by one proclamation (*jñaptidvitīya*), or a motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapticaturtha*). This is called the legal issue concerning duties.
[The legal issue concerning disputes (*vivādādhikaraṇa*) follows.]
"Monks, what is the root of a legal dispute concerning contention (*vivādādhikaraṇa*), and what is the root of such a dispute?
There are six roots of contention and fourteen matters that cause schism. What are the six roots of contention?"
For example, suppose here someone is prone to anger and harbors resentment;
being prone to anger and resentful, he does not honor, revere, esteem, or worship the Teacher.
Not honoring, revering, esteeming, or worshipping the Teacher, he does not see the Dharma.

Not seeing the Dharma, he becomes indifferent toward the state of a recluse (*śrāmaṇya*); being indifferent toward the state of a recluse, he engenders such strife within the Saṅgha as quarreling, brawling, contention, and dispute— whatever quarreling, brawling, contention, and dispute there may be that leads to the harm of many people, the detriment of many people, the suffering of many people, and to the harm, detriment, and suffering of gods and humans.

"Monks, if you perceive such a root of dispute— whether internal or external— to be unabandoned, then you, being united, harmonious, living in mutual joy, and free from contention, must apply yourselves with intense desire, energy, exertion, enthusiasm, fortitude, and indefatigable mindfulness and clear comprehension, in order to abandon that very root of dispute once it has arisen."

And in this way, you will abandon that root of dispute. Monks, if you perceive such a root of dispute— whether internal or external— to have been abandoned, then there, being united, harmonious, living in mutual joy, and free from dispute, you should apply intense desire, energy, and exertion.
With energy, perseverance, and non-opposition, you should apply mindfulness and clear comprehension so that this very root of dispute, once abandoned, will not flow forth again in the future;
thus it is for you. (Adhik-v 73)

That root of dispute, when properly and thoroughly restrained, will not arise in the future— such as one who is angry, resentful, deceitful, malicious, envious, stingy, crafty, guileful, shameless, lacking in dread of blame, having evil desires, and holding wrong views; furthermore, in this case, some person is personally attached to their own views, grasping at what is improper, and possesses counsel that is difficult to relinquish.
He who himself clings to his own views and is a counselor of evil wisdom does not honor, revere, esteem, or worship the Teacher;
by not honoring, revering, esteeming, or worshipping the Teacher, he does not see the Dharma;
not seeing the Dharma, he becomes indifferent to the state of a recluse.
Disregarding the life of a recluse, he creates such strife within the Saṅgha—

quarrels, brawls, disputes, and contention— that which is a quarrel, brawl, dispute, and contention for the harm of many people, for the detriment of many people, for the suffering of many people, and for the harm, detriment, and suffering of gods and humans. Monks, if you perceive such a root of dispute, whether internal or external, as not yet abandoned, [you must strive to eliminate it].

In this regard, you should all, united, harmonious, and living in mutual joy without dispute, apply yourselves with intense desire, vigor, exertion, enthusiasm, fortitude, and indefatigability, through mindfulness and clear comprehension, for the sake of abandoning this very root of dispute once it has arisen.
In this way, you will abandon that root of dispute;
if, monks, you perceive such a root of dispute— whether internal or external— as abandoned.

In this regard, you must all, united, harmonious, and living in mutual joy without dispute, apply yourselves with intense desire, vigor, exertion, enthusiasm, fortitude, and indefatigability, through mindfulness and clear comprehension, until this very root of dispute is abandoned so that it does not flow forth again in the future.
In this way, that root of dispute of yours, being thoroughly and correctly settled, will not arise again in the future.
These are called the six roots of dispute.
What are the fourteen matters that cause schism? [They are as follows:]... [list] ...these are the fourteen matters that cause schism.
Namely: whether it be called "Dharma" or "non-Dharma," "Vinaya" or "non-Vinaya," "an offense" or "no offense."
Whether it be heavy or light,
with remainder or without remainder, requiring instruction or requiring restraint, leading to ill-spoken words or leading to well-spoken words;

These are called the fourteen matters that cause schism; monks, this is the root of a legal dispute arising from contention, and this is the root of a legal dispute arising from contention. [The legal procedure concerning non-instruction.]

"Monks, what is the root of a legal issue concerning non-instruction? What is the root of a legal issue concerning non-instruction? That which is the Sangha’s non-instruction, its failure to instruct, and its refusal to institute instruction—based upon that, whatever quarreling, brawling, strife, and dispute arises: monks, this is the root of a legal issue concerning non-instruction; this is the root of a legal issue concerning non-instruction."
"O monks, what is the root of the legal issue concerning offenses (*āpattyadhikaraṇa*)? What is the root of the legal issue concerning offenses?"
The collection of offenses consisting of five types of offenses is called the "aggregate of offenses.
Which five?
The *pārājika* offenses, the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, the *pāyattika* offenses, the *pratideśanīya* offenses, and the *duṣkṛta* offenses.
Furthermore, there is an offense that is physical, but neither vocal nor mental;
there is one that is vocal, but neither physical nor mental;
and there is one that is both physical and mental, but not vocal.
There is an offense that is vocal and mental but not physical;
there is one that is physical, vocal, and mental.
What is an offense that is physical but neither vocal nor mental?

For example, when householders and those not yet ordained have not departed, a monk prepares his bed while thinking, "The householders and those not yet ordained have departed," and a woman lies down with him while he is asleep, or he is placed upon a large couch while asleep—
this is an offense that is physical, neither vocal nor mental.
What is an offense that is vocal, neither physical nor mental?
It is, for example, when a monk, while teaching the Dharma to a woman using five points, unintentionally exceeds the sixth point;
or when teaching using six points, he exceeds the seventh point.
This offense is vocal, not physical, and not mental.
What offense is both physical and mental, but not vocal?
For example, when a monk intentionally deprives a living being belonging to the animal realm of life, it is not thus [vocal].
He said: "A living being should be deprived of life in this way: just as I have deprived him of life, so too should he be deprived of life; when he has been deprived of life, it is well-deprived."
Taking what is not given, engaging in sexual misconduct, or drinking intoxicants, one does not say:
"Intoxicants should be drunk in this manner;
just as they were drunk by me, so too should intoxicants be drunk again."
"It has been drunk, it has been well drunk"—
this is an offense that is physical and mental, not verbal.
What is an offense that is verbal and mental, not physical?
For example, when a monk, while teaching the Dharma to a woman using five points, intentionally exceeds the sixth point, or while teaching using six points, exceeds the seventh point—
this is an offense that is both vocal and mental, but not physical. What is an offense that is physical, vocal, and mental?
For example, a monk intentionally deprives a living being belonging to the animal realm of life and says:
"A living being should be deprived of life in this manner;
just as it has been deprived by me, so too, if it were deprived in this way, it would have been well-deprived."
Taking what is not given, engaging in sexual misconduct, and drinking intoxicants, he says: "Intoxicants should indeed be drunk in this way;
for just as they were drunk by me, so too when drunk again, they become well-drunk."
This offense is bodily, vocal, and mental;
monks, this is the root of the legal issue concerning offenses,
and this is the root of the legal issue concerning offenses.
What is the root of the legal issue concerning duties (*kṛtyādhikaraṇa*)? Monks, the legal issue concerning duties— what is the root of the legal issue concerning duties?

Whatever formal act of the Saṃgha there is—whether a motion (*jñapti*), a motion followed by one proclamation (*jñaptidvitīya*), or a motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapticaturtha*)—this, O monks, is the legal question concerning duties (*kṛtyādhikaraṇa*) rooted therein; this is the root of the legal question concerning duties.
Regarding the three kinds of legal questions concerning disputes (*vivādādhikaraṇa*):
O monks, a legal question concerning disputes should be declared as wholesome (*kuśala*), unwholesome (*akuśala*), or indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Which is wholesome?

That which consists of various disputes, quarrels, and contradictory statements on the part of one who seeks the welfare of the Saṅgha, who intends for its welfare, who seeks what is wholesome, and who intends for what is wholesome—on account of that, whatever strife, wrangling, contention, and dispute there may be: this is wholesome.

What is unwholesome? That which is the speaking at variance, the quarreling, the discordant speech, the strife, the bickering, the contention, and the dispute of one who seeks the harm of the Saṅgha, who intends harm, who seeks what is unwholesome, and who intends what is unwholesome— this, based upon that, is unwholesome.
What is the indeterminate?
That which is neither for the benefit nor for the non-benefit of the Saṅgha; neither intended for its benefit nor intended for its non-benefit;
neither seeking what is wholesome nor seeking what is unwholesome; neither having a wholesome intention nor having an unwholesome intention; it is a discordant speech.
Dispute (*vivāda*) is contrary speech; based upon that, whatever quarreling, brawling, contention, or dispute there is—this is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Regarding the three types of *anavavādādhikaraṇa*: the *anavavādādhikaraṇa* should be stated as wholesome (*kuśala*), unwholesome (*akuśala*), or indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

Which is wholesome? That which consists of quarreling, brawling, strife, and dispute arising from the failure to instruct, the failure to provide instruction, and the failure to initiate instruction on behalf of a Saṅgha that desires what is beneficial, intends what is beneficial, seeks what is wholesome, and intends what is wholesome— this is wholesome.
Which is unwholesome?

That which—on account of not instructing, not admonishing, and not establishing instruction for one who is hostile toward the Saṅgha, who intends harm toward the Saṅgha, who seeks what is unwholesome, and who intends what is unwholesome—the quarreling, strife, contention, and dispute that arise: this is unwholesome.
What is the indeterminate?
It is that which is neither for the benefit nor for the harm of the Saṅgha; it is neither intended for its benefit nor intended for its harm;
it is not for one seeking the wholesome, nor for one seeking the unwholesome; it is neither with a wholesome intention nor with an unwholesome intention; it is non-instruction.
Lack of instruction and the failure to initiate instruction—based on that, whatever quarreling, bickering, conflict, or dispute arises, this is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Regarding the two types of legal issues concerning offenses (*āpattyadhikaraṇa*):
it should be stated that a legal issue concerning an offense may be unwholesome (*akuśala*) or it may be indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

Which is unwholesome? That which is a deliberate transgression of the training prescribed by the Buddha and the practice prescribed for the Saṅgha—this is unwholesome. Which [is wholesome]? (Adhik-v 77)

What is the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)? That which is an unintentional transgression regarding the training prescribed by the Buddha and the conduct prescribed for the Saṃgha—this is the indeterminate.
Regarding the three types of legal issues arising from business (*kṛtyādhikaraṇa*): it should be stated whether a legal issue arising from business is wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.

Which is the wholesome? That which, based upon a formal motion (*jñapti*), a motion followed by one proclamation (*jñaptidvitīya*), or a formal act following four proclamations (*jñapticaturtha*)— performed for the sake of the Saṅgha, with the intention for its welfare, seeking what is wholesome, and intending what is wholesome— the quarreling, strife, contention, and dispute that arise therefrom.
This is wholesome;
what is unwholesome?
It is the formal motion (*jñapti*) made by one who desires harm for the Saṅgha, who intends harm, who desires what is unwholesome, and who intends what is unwholesome.

Taking as a basis a formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya*) or a motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha*), whatever quarrel, strife, contention, or dispute arises—this is unwholesome (*akuśala*).
Which is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?
That which belongs to the Saṅgha which is neither desirous nor undesirous [of the outcome], neither having the intention for gain nor having the intention for loss.

Neither for one seeking the wholesome nor for one seeking the unwholesome, neither for one with a wholesome intention nor for one with an unwholesome intention, is there an act consisting of a motion (*jñapti*), a motion followed by a second [proclamation], or an act consisting of a motion followed by a fourth [proclamation]; based upon that, there is quarreling, brawling, strife, and dispute—this is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Not all types of dispute are [indeterminate].
And so forth:
are the sources of *adhikaraṇa* the same as the *adhikaraṇa* itself, such that whatever is the dispute (*vivāda*) is the *adhikaraṇa*, and whatever is the *adhikaraṇa* is the dispute?
He said: There may be a dispute that is not a legal case; there may be a legal case that is not a dispute;
there may be both a dispute and a legal case.
There may be neither dispute nor legal case:
1) first, a dispute is not a legal case when it is the discordant speech and opposing speech of the Saṃgha; 2) [and so forth].
A legal case (*adhikaraṇa*) is not a dispute (*vivāda*);

there are three types of legal cases: the legal case concerning censure (*anavavādādhikaraṇa*), the legal case concerning offenses (*āpattyadhikaraṇa*), and the legal case concerning duties (*kṛtyādhikaraṇa*).
3) And disputes are also legal cases.

That which is the Sangha’s speaking at variance, quarreling, opposing speech, lack of concord, lack of harmony, and state of division—on account of that, whatever strife, wrangling, contention, and dispute there may be; 4) there may be neither dispute nor legal issue, setting aside these aforementioned modes. (Adhik-v 78)
Is that which is non-admonition a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*), or is that which is a legal issue non-admonition?
He replied: There may be non-admonition that is not a legal issue; there may be a legal issue that is not non-admonition.
There may be non-instruction and a legal dispute; there may be neither non-instruction nor a legal dispute.
1) First, there is non-instruction that is not a legal dispute.

1) That which is the Sangha’s non-instruction, non-instructing, and non-establishment of instruction; 2) legal cases (*adhikaraṇa*) are not non-instruction, for there are three legal cases: the legal case of dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*), the legal case of offense (*āpattyadhikaraṇa*), and the legal case of business (*kṛtyādhikaraṇa*); 3)
Non-instruction and legal dispute:
that which is the Sangha’s non-instruction, the state of non-instruction, and the instigation of non-instruction—based upon these, whatever quarreling, strife, contention, and dispute arises;
4) neither non-instruction nor legal dispute.
Setting aside these modes, is whatever offense is a legal case (*adhikaraṇa*), or whatever is a legal case an offense?
He said: There may be an offense that is not a legal case.
There may be a legal case that is not an offense; there may be both an offense and a legal case; and there may be neither an offense nor a legal case. 1)

First, an offense (*āpatti*) is not itself a legal case (*adhikaraṇa*); rather, the five classes of offenses—the groups of offenses (*āpattinikāya*)—are called the "masses of offenses" (*āpattiskandha*), namely: those involving defeat (*pārājika*), formal meetings of the community (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*), offenses requiring expiation with forfeiture (*pāyattika*), offenses requiring confession (*pratideśanika*), and minor offenses (*duṣkṛta*).
Second, a legal case is not an offense.

There are three types of legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*): the legal issue of dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*), the legal issue of censure (*anavavādādhikaraṇa*), and the legal issue of business (*kṛtyādhikaraṇa*). (3) Furthermore, an offense (*āpatti*) and a legal issue constitute what is called the "five classes of offenses" (*pañcāpattijāti*), the "groups of offenses" (*āpattinikāya*), or the "aggregates of offenses" (*āpattiskandha*).

There are offenses involving defeat (*pārājika*), formal meetings of the community (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*), expiation with forfeiture (*pāyattika*), confession (*pratideśanika*), and wrongdoings (*duṣkṛta*);
based upon these, there arise quarreling, strife, contention, and dispute. 4)
Is there neither an offense nor a legal case?
Setting aside these modes,
is that which is a duty (kṛtya) a legal case (adhikaraṇa), or is that which is a legal case a duty?
He said: There may be a legal task that is not a formal dispute;
there may be a formal dispute that is not a legal task; and there may be both a legal task and a formal dispute.
There may be that which is neither a formal act (*kṛtya*) nor a legal procedure (*adhikaraṇa*):

1) first, that which is a formal act but not a legal procedure, namely a motion (*jñapti*), a motion followed by one proclamation (*jñaptidvitīya*), or a motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapticaturtha*) performed by the Saṃgha; 2) [and so forth].
Legal cases (*adhikaraṇa*) are not necessarily matters for action (*kṛtya*);
there are three types of legal cases: the legal case of dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*), the legal case of censure (*anavavādādhikaraṇa*), and the legal case of offense (*āpattyadhikaraṇa*).
(3) There are also those that are both matters for action and legal cases.

Whatever dispute, quarrel, contention, or conflict arises based on a formal act of the Saṃgha— whether it be a motion (*jñapti*), a motion followed by one proclamation (*jñaptidvitīya*), or a formal act following four proclamations (*jñapticaturtha*)—
that is neither a formal duty (*kṛtya*) nor a legal case (*adhikaraṇa*),
setting aside these aforementioned modes. (Adhik-v 79)
The Settlement of Disputes:
Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana settle a dispute.
"Monks, by how many methods for settling legal issues (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha-dharma*) should a dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*) be subdued, pacified, and brought to complete cessation?"
He said: "By two means: by *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence) and by the taking of voting tickets (*śalākā*) by the majority.
How does *saṃmukhavinaya* become a settlement of legal issues (*adhikaraṇaśamatha*), and how do these legal issues attain their taming, pacification, and complete subsiding?"
That is to say, by means of the settlement of legal disputes through face-to-face confrontation.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, had entered the rains retreat at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍada;
meanwhile, a great number of monks had entered the rains retreat in the countryside.
During the rainy season, a quarrel, a scuffle, a conflict, and a dispute arose among them;
they entrusted that legal case to the venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana,
and those two settled that legal case in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction.

Then a great number of monks, having spent the rains retreat in the countryside and completed three months, having finished their robes and prepared their alms-bowls, set out on a journey toward Śrāvastī.
Traveling by stages along the road, they arrived at Śrāvastī.
Then those many monks, having put away their bowls and robes and washed their feet, approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, they sat down to one side;
for it is the nature of things that the Buddha-Blessed Ones greet visiting monks with this customary greeting:
"From where have you come now, monks, and where did you spend the rains retreat?
Thus the Blessed One greeted many monks with friendly inquiry:
"From where have you come?"
"Monks, come now; where have you spent the rains?
"Venerable sir, we have come from the countryside; we spent the rains in the countryside."
“Monks, I hope you have spent the rains retreat in comfort in the countryside and have not been distressed for lack of alms-food?

“Venerable Sir, we have indeed spent the rains retreat in comfort in the countryside and have not been distressed for lack of alms-food; however, during the rains, quarrels, strife, disputes, and contention arose among us.”

That legal case was entrusted by them to us, the venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana; and that legal case was settled by those two in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction.

The Blessed One perceived: "Alas, my resident disciples will be able to settle, as they arise, each legal dispute according to the Dharma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the Teacher's instruction."
"Therefore, monks, disputes as they arise should be settled by the monks dwelling on dry land in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction.
The monks did not know who were those dwelling on dry land or how many there were.
The Blessed One said:
Those who are able to settle whatever legal disputes arise within the Saṅgha are threefold:
there is one who stands on firm ground, yet is neither restrained in body nor in speech.
There is one who is restrained by body but not by speech;
there is one who is restrained by both body and speech.
Which one is neither restrained by body nor by speech?
It is as if a monk standing on dry land were to approach monks who have fallen into quarreling, brawling, conflict, and dispute, and who are divided into opposing factions, and say to them:
"It is well, venerable sirs! This legal issue has been correctly grasped, not wrongly grasped;
it is well-applied, not ill-applied; it is well-examined, not ill-examined. Speak thus and so, and do not speak otherwise."
"May the venerable ones crush the enemies;
may no enemy crush us; we are on the side of the venerable ones, their strength, and their allies"—thus, having approached the second party themselves, they spoke in this way.
He said: "Well done, venerable ones! This legal case has been well-grasped, not wrongly grasped; it is well-applied, not ill-applied; it is well-examined, not ill-examined.
Speak thus and thus; do not speak otherwise. Venerable ones, let you crush the opponents!"
"And let no other person overcome us; we are on the side of the venerable ones, their strength and their helpers"—
this man standing on dry land is neither restrained in body nor in speech.
What is one who stands on dry land, restrained in body but not in speech?

It is as follows: standing on dry land, when monks have fallen into quarreling, brawling, contention, and dispute, being divided into opposing factions, he does not personally approach one faction; rather, he sends a messenger, saying:
"Excellent, venerable ones! This legal case has been well-grasped, not wrongly grasped; it is well-applied, not ill-applied; it is well-examined, not poorly examined.
Speak thus and so, and do not speak otherwise.
May the venerable ones crush their opponents!"
"Let not another overpower us; we are on the side of the venerable ones, with them as our strength and allies"—
yet even in this second case, he does not approach [the matter] from his own perspective.

Rather, he sends a messenger, saying: "Venerable sirs, this legal case has been well-grasped by you, not poorly grasped; it is well-applied, not ill-applied; it is well-examined, not poorly examined. Speak thus and thus, and do not speak otherwise. Venerable sirs, let you crush the opponents!"
"Let not another overpower us, thinking: 'We are the faction, the strength, and the allies of the Venerable Ones';
this one stands on dry land, restrained in body but not in speech."
What is one who stands on firm ground, restrained in body and speech?

It is as follows: standing on firm ground, he does not personally approach monks who have fallen into quarrels, disputes, conflicts, and arguments, and who are divided into opposing factions, nor does he send a messenger.
A second time as well, he does not approach in person nor does he dispatch a messenger.

In this regard, one who stands on dry ground, being neither restrained in body nor in speech—such a person standing on dry ground, if unappointed, should not be appointed; and if already appointed, should be dismissed.
Why is that?

For when such a person established on dry land has arrived among the Saṅgha, legal disputes that have not yet arisen do arise, and those that have already arisen do not quickly reach pacification through the Dharma and the Vinaya.

In this regard, one who is established on dry land who is restrained in body but not in speech—such a person established on dry land, if unappointed, should not be appointed; and if already appointed, he should be removed from his office.
Why is that?

Even when such a person stands as a mediator, unarisen legal disputes arise within the Saṅgha, and those already arisen are quickly brought to pacification through the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction.
In that regard, this mediator who is restrained in body and speech—such a mediator, even if not yet appointed, should be appointed; and once appointed, he should not be dismissed.
For what reason? Because,

having come upon such a person standing firm, legal disputes (*adhikaraṇa*) that have not yet arisen do not arise within the Saṅgha, and those already arisen quickly reach pacification through the Dharma, through justice, and according to the Teacher’s instruction.

Monks, it is only those of such a kind who, standing on firm ground, are capable of settling legal disputes, and not others; by such as these, standing on firm ground, whatever legal disputes arise should be settled,
and by such as these, standing on firm ground, legal disputes have been settled.
Two presences: the person (pudgala) and the phenomenon (dharma);
that which is pure and present before one.
What is "face-to-face" here?
There are two kinds of face-to-face: face-to-face with persons and face-to-face with the Dharma.
What is face-to-face with the person (*pudgalasaṃmukha*)? It is those who settle that legal case; and all those by whom that legal case is settled must be assembled together and present in person.
This is called face-to-face with the person.
What is face-to-face with the Dharma?

It is when that legal issue is settled by means of that Dharma, by means of that discipline, and by means of that teaching of the Teacher. By means of that Dharma, by means of that discipline, and by means of that teaching of the Teacher, that legal issue [is resolved].
This is called "in the presence of the Dharma.
If the monks staying on dry land are unable to settle that legal dispute, they must entrust that legal dispute to the Saṃgha;
the Saṃgha must settle that legal dispute in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction.
That legal dispute has been settled by the Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction; it has been thoroughly pacified.
The three presences: the Saṃgha, the individual, and the Dharma.
The pure [attainment] is face-to-face.
What is face-to-face here?
There are three things that are face-to-face:
In the presence of the Saṅgha, in the presence of an individual, and in the presence of the Dharma.
What is "in the presence of the Saṃgha"? It is when as many monks as have reached the boundary and reached the [legal] action have all assembled and are present;
and consent has been brought from those who are entitled to give consent.
And when the monks have assembled and are present together, they do not resist and do not protest;
whereas for those who would resist and protest, their protest would prevail and they would perform [unwholesome] deeds—this is called "in the presence of the Saṃgha.
What is "in the presence of the individual"?
When those who settle that legal case and those for whom that legal case is settled are all assembled and present together—
this is called "presence of persons.
What is "presence of the Dharma"?
By whatever Dharma, by whatever Vinaya, and by whatever teaching of the Teacher that legal dispute (*adhikaraṇa*) is pacified— by that Dharma, by that Vinaya, and by that teaching of the Teacher—
that legal dispute is called "face-to-face with the Dharma" (*dharmasaṃmukha*).
If the Saṃgha is unable to pacify that legal dispute, then afterwards the Saṃgha should appoint monks who have been selected, whether they be ten or five.

Furthermore, they should be appointed in this manner: having prepared the seating and struck the gong, and having exhorted the monks with a formal inquiry, when the entire Saṃgha has assembled and is seated, they should first be encouraged thus:
"Are you, Buddharakṣita, Dharmadatta, and Saṃghasena, willing to go outside the boundary and, being formally constituted as a committee, settle a legal dispute for the Saṃgha?"
If they are able, they should say, "We are able.
Thereafter, one monk, having made a formal motion (*jñapti*), should perform the ritual act (*karman*):
"Listen, venerable Saṃgha! These Buddharakṣita, Dharmadatta, and Saṃghasena are prepared to go outside the boundary to settle the legal disputes of the Saṃgha."
If it seems appropriate to the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha should permit it, let the Saṃgha appoint Buddhārakṣita, Dharmadatta, and Saṃghasena as *vyūḍhakas*.
Buddhārakṣita, Dharmadatta, and Saṃghasena, as *vyūḍhakas*, are capable of going outside the boundary to settle legal disputes for the Saṃgha.
This is the motion (*jñapti*).
Thereafter, the formal act (karman) should be performed:

"May the venerable Saṃgha listen. These [monks], Buddharakṣita, Dharmadatta, and Saṃghasena, being qualified, are capable of going outside the boundary (sīmā) to settle the legal disputes of the Saṃgha.
Therefore, let the Saṃgha authorize Buddharakṣita, Dharmadatta, and Saṃghasena as qualified [mediators]."
Buddharakṣita, Dharmadatta, and Saṃghasena, being *vyūḍhaka*, shall go outside the boundary and settle the legal disputes of the Saṃgha.
To those venerable ones who approve of appointing Buddharakṣita, Dharmadatta, and Saṃghasena as *vyūḍhaka*:
"Buddharakṣita, Dharmadatta, and Saṃghasena, being *vyūḍhaka*, shall go outside the boundary and [settle] the legal disputes of the Saṃgha."
If you approve, remain silent; if you do not approve, speak up. The Saṃgha has authorized Buddharakṣitā, Dharmadattā, and Saṃghasenā as marshals.
"And having gone outside the boundary, they shall settle the legal disputes of the Saṅgha;
it is approved and authorized by the Saṅgha since there is silence;
thus do I hold this: that those legal disputes are to be settled by the *vyūḍhaka* [formal assembly] in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction."
That legal case should be declared as settled and thoroughly pacified by means of the Dharma, the Teacher’s instruction, through the *vyūḍhaka* procedure.
There are two [factors]: the person (*pudgala*) and the Dharma (*dharma*).
The pure face-to-face [confession]: what here is "face-to-face"?
There are two kinds of face-to-face.
It is face-to-face with persons and face-to-face with the Dharma.
What is face-to-face with persons? It is when all those who settle that legal case and those for whom that legal case is settled are assembled together and present in person.
This is called face-to-face with the person.
What is face-to-face with the Dharma?

It is that by which—by means of which Dharma, by means of which Vinaya, and by means of which teaching of the Teacher—that legal case is pacified; [it is] by that Dharma, by that Vinaya, and by that teaching of the Teacher.
They settle the legal case;
this is called "in the presence of the Dharma.
If the monks who have been drawn up in assembly are unable to settle that legal case, [they should proceed as follows].

Those monks who are *vyūḍhakavyūḍhaka*—eight or nine in number—should be appointed. That legal case (*adhikaraṇa*) must be settled by those *vyūḍhakavyūḍhaka* monks in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction.
When that legal case has been settled by the *vyūḍhakavyūḍhaka* monks, it should be declared as "well-settled."
If the monks who are experts in formal legal procedures (*vyūḍhaka-vyūḍhaka*) are unable to settle that legal dispute (*adhikaraṇa*), they must present that dispute before the Saṃgha.
Then, the Saṃgha should appoint a monk endowed with five qualities as the monk who transfers the legal dispute (*adhikaraṇa-saṃcāraka*).
A monk who has not been appointed as the transferer of legal disputes should not be appointed; and one who has been appointed should be dismissed if he lacks the necessary qualifications.
By which five?
He acts out of desire, he acts out of hatred, he acts out of delusion, he acts out of fear, and he does not know whether a legal case has been transferred or not transferred.
A monk endowed with these five qualities who is a transferer of legal cases—if unappointed, he should not be appointed; if already appointed, he should be dismissed.

A monk endowed with five qualities who is a conveyor of legal cases (*adhikaraṇasaṃcāraka*) should, if not yet appointed, be appointed; and if already appointed, he should not be dismissed. What are the five?
He does not act out of desire, nor out of hatred, nor out of delusion, nor out of fear. (Adhik-v 85)
He knows whether a legal case has been transferred or not transferred.
Endowed with these five qualities, a monk who transfers legal cases should be appointed even if not yet appointed, and once appointed, he should not be removed.
Furthermore, he should be appointed in this manner:
Having prepared the seats and beaten the ghaṇṭī, and having instructed the monks by means of a formal inquiry, when the entire Saṃgha has sat down and assembled, they should first be encouraged:
"Venerable ones, are you able to carry out the formal transfer of the legal case for the Saṃgha? If they are able, they should say, "We are able."

Thereafter, a single monk, having made a formal motion (*jñapti*), should perform the ritual act (*karman*): "Listen, venerable Saṃgha! This monk named so-and-so, the administrator of legal cases (*adhikaraṇasaṃcāraka*), is capable of administering the legal cases of the Saṃgha.
If it seems the right time to the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha permit that the Saṃgha should appoint this monk named so-and-so as the administrator of legal cases."
The monk named so-and-so shall transfer the legal case for the Saṃgha; this is the motion;
the formal act (karman) is to be performed.
"Listen, venerable Saṃgha!
This monk named so-and-so, the administrator of legal cases, is capable of administering a legal case for the Saṃgha.

Therefore, let the Saṃgha appoint this monk named so-and-so as the administrator of legal cases; this monk named so-and-so, the administrator of legal cases, shall administer a legal case for the Saṃgha."
Those venerable ones who approve of appointing the monk named so-and-so as the conveyor of legal cases—
that the monk named so-and-so, as the conveyor of legal cases, shall convey the legal case for the Saṅgha—
let them remain silent; those who do not approve, [speak].
Let it be spoken: the Saṃgha has approved the monk named so-and-so as the administrator of legal cases;
he shall administer the legal case for the Saṃgha. It is accepted and authorized by the Saṃgha, since there is silence.

I shall maintain this: I prescribe the customary duties for a monk who is a conveyor of legal cases (*adhikaraṇasaṃcāraka*). A monk who is a conveyor of legal cases must present this case before the Saṃgha together with its elders and the Prātimokṣa, and he must report it exactly as it occurred.
Listen, venerable Saṃgha!
"This legal case arose in this residence concerning this matter after such a length of time;
that legal case could not be settled by the monks staying on the spot;
they therefore referred it to the Saṃgha."
The Saṃgha was not able [to settle the matter]; therefore, the monks who were selected as "dividers" (vyūḍhaka) were appointed;
yet even those divided monks were not able [to do so].
By them also, monks who were *vyūḍhakavyūḍhaka* were appointed; by those *vyūḍhakavyūḍhaka* monks also, [the matter] was entrusted to the Saṃgha;
and by the Saṃgha also...
"I, the monk named so-and-so, have been appointed as the administrator of legal cases (*adhikaraṇasaṃcāraka*).

I, the monk named so-and-so, the administrator of legal cases, entrust this legal case to the Saṃgha together with its elders and the Prātimokṣa. May the venerable Saṃgha bring it to resolution, up until the limit of six months; that legal case must be settled by the Saṃgha together with its elders and the Prātimokṣa, in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction."

It should be said that the legal case has been settled by the Saṃgha together with its elders and together with the Prātimokṣa, in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction.
The three presences are: the Saṃgha, the individual (pudgala), and the Dharma.
The pure [action] is "in the presence of"; what is meant here by "in the presence of"?
There are three kinds of presence: presence before the Saṃgha, presence before an individual, and presence before the Dharma.
What is "in the presence of the Saṃgha"? It is when as many monks as have reached the boundary and reached the [legal] action have all assembled and are present;
and consent has been brought from those who are entitled to give consent.

And when the monks have assembled and are present face-to-face, they do not resist and do not protest; whereas for those who resist and protest, their protest takes root and they perform [obstructive] actions—this is called "in the presence of the Saṃgha.
What is "in the presence of the individual" (pudgala-saṃmukha)?
When those who settle that legal case and those for whom that legal case is settled are all assembled and present together, this is called "presence of persons" (*pudgalasammukha*).
What is "presence of the Dharma" (*dharmasammukha*)?
It is when that legal case is settled by means of that Dharma, that Vinaya, and that teaching of the Teacher.
When they settle that legal case by means of that Dharma, by means of that Vinaya, and by means of that teaching of the Teacher, this is called "face-to-face with the Dharma" (*dharmasaṃmukha*).
If the Saṅgha, together with its elders and its Prātimokṣa, is unable to settle that legal case, it should entrust that legal case to a monk who is a conveyor of legal cases (*adhikaraṇasaṃcāraka*).
That monk, the conveyor of legal cases, should then entrust it to monks who are experts in the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkās.
And it should be reported exactly as it occurred:
"Listen, O venerable monks who uphold the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkās:
this legal dispute arose in that residence concerning that matter at such a length of time ago."
That legal case could not be settled by the monks staying on the ground;
they handed it over to the Saṃgha,
but even the Saṃgha was unable to settle it.
By him, too, the *vyūḍhaka* monks were appointed;
by those *vyūḍhaka* monks, it was not possible [to settle the matter];
by them, too, the *vyūḍhakavyūḍhaka* monks were appointed.
Even by the monks arranged in double arrays it was not possible;
they too deposited it with the Saṃgha.

I, the monk named so-and-so, have been appointed by the Saṃgha as the monk who transmits legal cases; therefore, this legal case has been entrusted to me, the monk named so-and-so acting as the transmitter of legal cases, by the Saṃgha together with its elders and its Prātimokṣa; and it has likewise been entrusted to me, the monk named so-and-so acting as the transmitter of legal cases, by the Saṃgha together with its elders and its Prātimokṣa.
I, the monk named [so-and-so], acting as a conveyor of legal cases, entrust this legal case to the monks who are holders of the Sūtras,
the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkās. May you, venerable monks who are holders of the Sūtras,
the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkās, settle this legal case for a period of one year.

That legal case (*adhikaraṇa*) must be settled by monks who are holders of the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkās, in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction. When that legal case has been settled by monks who are holders of the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkās, it should be declared as "well-settled.
The two presences (*dvau sannipātau*):
The person and the phenomena are pure and face-to-face; what here is "face-to-face"?
There are two types of presence: presence of persons and presence of the Dharma.
What is presence of persons?
It is when all those who settle that legal case and those for whom that legal case is settled are assembled together and present.
This is called "in the presence of the person.
What is "in the presence of the Dharma"?

It is when that legal case is settled by means of that Dharma, by means of that Vinaya, and by means of that teaching of the Teacher—by means of that Dharma, that Vinaya, and that teaching of the Teacher.
This is called "in the presence of the Dharma.

If the monks who are holders of the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Mātṛkās are unable to settle that legal case, they must entrust it to a monk designated as the "carrier of the legal case" (adhikaraṇasaṃcāraka).

That monk who is the carrier of the legal case must entrust it to whichever monastery has a monk who is either a senior elder (sthavira), or one of those most senior, or one who is renowned, or one of those most renowned.
And you must report exactly what occurred: "Listen, Elder, this legal case arose in such-and-such a residence at such-and-such a time concerning this very matter;
that legal case could not be settled by the monks staying on dry land."
They deposited it with the Saṃgha;
the Saṃgha was also unable [to settle it]; therefore, monks who were experts in legal procedures (*vyūḍhaka*) were appointed by him.
The monks who were *vyūḍhaka* were also not able [to perform the formal act];
the monks who were *vyūḍhakavyūḍhaka* were also authorized by them;
yet the monks who were *vyūḍhakavyūḍhaka* were also not able [to perform it].
It has been entrusted to the Saṃgha;
the Saṃgha, too, has approved me, the monk named so-and-so, as the monk who shall circulate the legal case.
In the Saṃgha...
This legal case has been entrusted by me, the monk named so-and-so, acting as the conveyor of legal cases, to the Saṃgha together with its elders and the Prātimokṣa.
It could not be settled by that Saṃgha together with its elders and the Prātimokṣa;
therefore, it was entrusted by them to me, the monk named so-and-so, acting as the conveyor of legal cases.

Therefore, that legal case was entrusted by me, the monk named so-and-so acting as the conveyor of the case, to monks who were experts in the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkās; yet even those experts were not able to resolve it, and they too entrusted it back to me, the monk named so-and-so acting as the conveyor of the case.
I, the monk named [Name], the administrator of legal cases, hand over this legal case to the Elder for him to settle, until its final conclusion.
I shall prescribe for the Elder, the monk, the rules of proper conduct.

The elder monk must not accept from the monks who are litigants or opponents the offering of tooth-sticks, nor cow dung, nor the bowl; he must not give them anything to eat or drink, nor engage in conversation with them, except when walking in front of or behind them.
This is what they should be told: "Venerable sirs, let there be no quarreling, no brawling, no strife, and no dispute.
For what reason?
Venerable sirs, for two who are disputing, there is no victory."
Rather, there is victory for one and defeat for the other;
there is no victory for two who are fighting together.

Rather, the elder monk should settle that legal case according to the Dharma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the Teacher’s instruction, such that there is victory for one and defeat for the other;
when the elder monk has settled that legal case, it should be declared that it has been well-settled.
For in this way, monks, there is the settlement of legal disputes through face-to-face resolution;
and furthermore, in this way, for certain legal disputes, there is taming, pacification, and complete subsiding, namely, by means of the settlement of legal disputes through face-to-face resolution.

And how, monks, does the settlement of legal questions (*adhikaraṇa*) by the taking of voting tickets by the majority (*yadbhūyaiṣīka-śalākāgrahaṇa*) come about? And how is there the taming, the pacification, and the complete subsiding of certain legal questions— namely, through the settlement of legal questions by the taking of voting tickets by the majority?
As before, beginning with those staying on the ground up to the *sthavira*;
if the *sthavira* monk is unable to settle that legal case (*adhikaraṇa*), he must hand over that legal case to that very monk who is the conveyor of legal cases; by him also...
That legal case should be submitted to the Saṃgha;

the Saṃgha should settle that legal case by means of the settlement of disputes through the drawing of lots according to the majority. There are five reasons why the settlement of disputes by the drawing of lots according to the majority is harsh, fierce, intense, suspicious of schism, and characterized by a lack of reversal in its application.
And how is one harsh? One is harsh when one is seized harshly by monks who are litigants or adversaries; thus is one harsh.
How is one "fierce"? The monks who are litigants and adversaries are fierce and aggressive;
thus is one fierce.
How is he firmly seized? He is firmly seized by monks who are litigants or opponents; thus is he firmly seized.
How does one become apprehensive of schism?
One thoroughly and correctly grasps any one of the fourteen things that cause schism;
in this way, one becomes apprehensive of schism.
How does one become one whose application is irreversible?
Beginning from those standing on firm ground up to the elder,
in this way one becomes one whose application is irreversible.
