A monk who possesses these five qualities— one who seeks the majority, who is capable of taking up the voting sticks for the purpose of settling a dispute, who is firm, who is fierce, who is resolute, and who suspects a schism and does not turn back from his application— should be appointed as the distributor of the voting sticks (*śalākācāraka*).
A monk who possesses five qualities who has not been appointed as the distributor of the voting sticks should not be appointed, and one who has been appointed should be dismissed.
By which five?
He goes out of desire, he goes out of hatred, he goes out of delusion, he goes out of fear, and he does not know whether the voting sticks have been distributed or not.
A monk who possesses these five qualities, though appointed as a distributor of voting sticks, should not be appointed if unappointed, and if already appointed, he should be removed from his office.
A monk endowed with five qualities who acts as the distributor of voting tickets (*śalākācāraka*), though not yet appointed, should be appointed; and once appointed, he should not be dismissed.
What are these five?
He does not act out of desire, nor out of hatred, nor out of delusion, nor out of fear; he acts according to what has been distributed and what has not been distributed.

And he knows the voting stick (*śalākā*). Endowed with these five qualities, a monk who distributes the voting sticks, though not yet appointed, should be appointed; and once appointed, he should not be dismissed. The Four Methods of Voting: 1. One who is a partisan (*pakṣika*) may distribute the voting sticks for one side. 2. One who is a partisan may distribute the voting sticks for both sides. 3. One who is impartial (*apakṣika*) may distribute the voting sticks for one side. 4. One who is impartial may distribute the voting sticks for both sides.
There are four ways of distributing voting tickets (*śalākā*);
which four?
Secret, open, with a whisper in the ear, and for the entire Saṃgha.
What is concealed voting by means of counting sticks (*śalākācāraṇa*)?

It is as follows: it occurs when a monk who is about to distribute the voting sticks thinks, "In this very residence there are many elder monks who speak contrary to the Dharma, whereas there are few junior monks who speak in accordance with the Dharma."
"If I were to distribute the voting sticks (*śalākā*) in public, it is possible that the junior monks, following the senior monks, might cast many illegal sticks.
What if I were to distribute the sticks in private? Thinking thus, he distributes the sticks in private;
this is called the "private distribution of sticks" (*channa-śalākā-cāraṇa*).
What is the open distribution of tickets (*śalākācāraṇa*)?
It is as follows: a monk who is distributing tickets thinks, "In this residence there are many elder monks who speak according to the Dharma, but few junior monks who speak contrary to the Dharma."
"If I were to distribute the voting sticks in secret, it is possible that the junior monks might take up sticks representing what is not the Dharma.
Suppose, then, I were to distribute the voting sticks openly.
When distributing the voting sticks openly, it is possible that the junior monks, following the example of the elder monks, will take up a great many sticks representing the Dharma."
When he moves the probe in an open [wound], this is called moving the probe in an open [wound]. What is moving the probe with a "karṇatuntunaka" [probe]?
Just as a monk acting as the distributor of voting-slips goes to the ear and whispers,
"Venerable one, the Dharma-voting slip has been taken by your preceptor;
you too should take a Dharma-voting slip."

"The teacher, the co-student, the co-instructor, the one with whom one has conversed, the one with whom one has talked intimately, the one who is well-acquainted, and the one who is affectionate—they have taken these dharma-voting sticks;
you too, take a dharma-voting stick.
This is called the practice of voting with sticks accompanied by whispering.
What is the distribution of voting sticks for the entire Saṅgha?
It is as follows: it occurs when this thought arises in the mind of the monk who distributes the voting sticks:
"In this residence, there are many monks who are ill."

"If I were to distribute voting tickets while the entire Saṅgha is neither seated nor assembled, it is possible that many monks might take tickets for what is not the Dharma; therefore, I shall not distribute the voting tickets until the entire Saṅgha is seated and assembled.
Having said this, he distributes the voting tickets once the entire Saṅgha is seated and assembled.
This is called the distribution of voting tickets for the entire Saṅgha. There are ten unlawful ways of taking voting tickets (*daśa adhārmikāṇi śalākāgrahaṇāni*).
There are ten lawful and ten unlawful ways of taking voting tickets (*ṣalākā*). What are they?
They take the voting ticket unlawfully.
They take voting sticks while distracted;
they take voting sticks for the sake of even a slight or minor matter;
they take voting sticks out of fear of schism.
They take the voting sticks with an irreversible application; they do not take the voting sticks as if acting as a charioteer who guides from one state to another;
rather, they take the voting sticks thinking, "By this taking of the voting sticks, the Saṃgha will be split."

Thinking, "Perhaps by the taking of the voting sticks, there will be even more monks who speak what is not the Dharma," they take the voting sticks while knowing that the Saṅgha will be split by the taking of the voting sticks;
thinking, "Perhaps by the taking of the voting sticks, there will be even more monks who speak what is not the Dharma," they take the voting sticks.
How do they take the voting sticks unlawfully?
They take the voting sticks not in accordance with the Vinaya;
thus they take the voting sticks unlawfully.
How do they take voting sticks while being divided?
They do not take the voting stick in the unity of the Saṃgha; thus they take the voting stick while being divided.
How do they take a voting stick with even a very slight or minor offense?
Knowing that it is something requiring restraint and something requiring confession, they take the voting stick.
Thus they take the voting stick with only a slight degree of inferiority.
How do those fearing a schism take the voting stick?
They have properly, thoroughly, and well grasped one or another of the fourteen matters that cause a schism.
Thus, those fearing a schism take the voting sticks (*śalākā*).
How do they take the voting sticks by means of an uninterrupted procedure? Not starting with those standing on dry land, nor until the Elder has taken his.
In this way they take the voting stick by means of an irreversible application.
How do they not take the voting stick by way of being a driver who has mastered the course?
Those monks who are holders of the Sūtras, holders of the Vinaya, and holders of the Mātṛkās are called "the courses" in that Dharma and Vinaya.
The attendants, having observed them, take up the voting sticks;

they do not take up the voting sticks by way of being attendants who follow the movement [of others]. Do they take up the voting sticks thinking, "In some way or other, by this taking up of the voting sticks, the Saṃgha will be split"? They take up the voting sticks [for that purpose].

They take up the voting sticks with the thought, "Perhaps by taking up these voting sticks, the Saṃgha will fall into schism"; likewise, they take up the voting sticks thinking, "In this way, by taking up the voting sticks, the Saṃgha will be split."
Do they take up the voting sticks thinking, "By taking up these sticks, perhaps a greater number of monks will become speakers of what is not Dharma"?
Do they take up the voting sticks thinking, "By taking up these sticks, perhaps a greater number of monks will persist in adopting what is not Dharma"?
Likewise, do they take up the voting sticks thinking, "By taking up these sticks, perhaps a greater number of monks will become speakers of what is not Dharma"?
How is it that they take voting sticks knowing, "The Saṅgha will be split by the taking of the voting sticks"?
They take the voting sticks with the thought, "The Saṅgha will go to schism by the taking of the voting sticks";
thus, knowing, "The Saṅgha will be split by the taking of the voting sticks," they take the voting sticks.
How is it that they take up the voting sticks while knowing, "By taking up these voting sticks, the majority of monks will be speakers of what is not Dharma"?
They take up the voting sticks with such a thought: "By taking up these voting sticks, the majority of monks will persist in adopting what is not Dharma."
Knowing thus, they take the voting sticks [thinking], "By taking the voting sticks, the majority of monks will be speakers of what is not Dharma";
these are the ten illegal distributions of voting sticks.
The ten distributions of voting sticks that are legal:
What are the ten lawful ways of taking voting tickets (*śalākā*)?
They take the ticket lawfully; they take the ticket while being in full assembly.
They do not take the voting stick for a mere trifle or a small matter;
they do not take the voting stick out of fear of schism; they do not take the voting stick by means of a deceptive maneuver.
They take the voting sticks because they are skilled in discerning the various courses of action;
nor do they take the voting sticks thinking, "By taking these sticks, the Saṅgha will be split";
nor do they take the voting sticks thinking, "By taking these sticks, more monks will become speakers of what is not the Dharma."
Do they take the voting sticks knowing that the Saṅgha will be split by the taking of the voting sticks?
Nor do they take the voting sticks knowing that, by the taking of the voting sticks, a greater number of monks will become speakers of what is not Dharma?
How then do they take the voting sticks in accordance with the Dharma?
They take the voting sticks in accordance with the Vinaya; thus they take the voting sticks according to the Dharma.
How do they take the voting sticks as a united assembly?
They take the voting sticks (*śalākā*) with the harmony of the Saṃgha;
how is it that they do not take the voting sticks for the sake of something merely trifling?
They do not take voting sticks thinking, "This requires neither restraint nor confession";
thus they do not take voting sticks for even a slight or minor matter.
How is it that they do not take voting sticks while suspecting a schism?
Among the fourteen grounds for causing schism, one or another ground for causing schism has been properly and thoroughly grasped;
thus, those who do not suspect a schism do not take a voting stick.
How is it that they do not take a voting stick by means of a deceptive maneuver?
Starting from those standing on the ground up to the elder;
thus they do not take the voting-ticket by means of a reversed application.
How then do they take the voting-ticket by means of being a charioteer who knows the various paths?
Those monks who are holders of the Sūtras, holders of the Vinaya, and holders of the Mātṛkās are called "those who have reached the goal" within that Dharma and Vinaya;
the charioteers, having observed them, take the voting sticks.
Thus, by virtue of being charioteers who have reached the goal, they take the voting sticks.
They take up the voting sticks with the thought, "The Saṅgha will not be split by this taking up of the voting sticks";

they take up the voting sticks with the thought, "The Saṅgha will certainly not reach a schism through this taking up of the voting sticks"; thus they take up the voting sticks with the thought, "The Saṅgha will certainly not be split by this taking up of the voting sticks."
They do not take up the voting sticks thinking, "By taking up these voting sticks, will not even more monks become speakers of what is not Dharma?
Nor do they take up the voting sticks thinking, "By taking up these voting sticks, will not even more monks persist in adopting what is not Dharma?
Likewise, they do not take up the voting sticks thinking, "By taking up these voting sticks, will not even more monks become speakers of what is not Dharma?"
How is it that they take up the voting sticks without knowing, "The Saṅgha will be split by the taking up of these voting sticks"?
They take up the voting sticks with the thought, "The Saṅgha will not go to schism by the taking up of these voting sticks";
thus, without knowing, "The Saṅgha will be split by the taking up of these voting sticks," they take up the voting sticks.

How is it that they take the voting sticks not knowing that by taking the sticks, the majority of monks will be speakers of what is not Dharma; nor do they take the sticks with the thought, "By taking the sticks, the majority of monks will persist in adopting what is not Dharma"? It is thus that they take the sticks.
Thus, knowing that by means of the drawing of lots (*śalākā*) many more monks will become speakers of what is not Dharma, they take up the lot.
These are the ten lawful ways of taking up the lot;
I shall now prescribe the rules of customary conduct for the monk who distributes the lots.
Regarding the methods of voting by means of *śalākā* (voting sticks), there are two kinds for the monks: the *śalākā* should be presented in two ways.
There are voting sticks for the Dharma and voting sticks for non-Dharma. The voting stick for the Dharma is straight, not crooked,
not bent, beautiful, and pleasant to the touch.
The non-dharma voting sticks are crooked, bent, curved, discolored, and unpleasant to the touch; therefore,

the monk acting as the distributor of the voting sticks, having taken up the dharma voting sticks with his right hand and the non-dharma voting sticks with his left, should stand before the senior of the Saṅgha and describe the qualities of the dharma voting sticks.
And there was disapproval of the non-dharma sticks:
"Venerable sir, take these dharma sticks, which are straight, not crooked, not curved, beautiful in color, and pleasant to the touch;
but take these non-dharma sticks, which are crooked, curved, twisted, ugly in color, and painful to the touch."
If he extends his hand with the voting stick for non-dharma,
it should not be granted on the first utterance, nor should it be granted on the second utterance.
On the third day, it should be given;
the Elder of the Saṃgha should confess the offense of a *duṣkṛta* for transgressing the Vinaya.

In this manner, up until standing before the youngest member of the Saṃgha, the praise of the dharma-voting sticks (*dharma-śalākā*) and the dispraise of the non-dharma voting sticks (*adharma-śalākā*) should be proclaimed.

"Take these Dharma voting-sticks, which are straight, not crooked, not curved, beautiful in color, and pleasant to the touch; but take these non-Dharma voting-sticks, which are crooked, bent, curved, ugly in color, and unpleasant to the touch.
If he extends his hand toward the non-Dharma voting-sticks, then on the first announcement, [the motion] shall not be granted."
It should not be given on the second day;
it should be given on the third day.
In this manner, the offense of a *duṣkṛta* that transgresses the Vinaya must be confessed by means of a ninefold assembly of the Saṃgha.
If the voting sticks for the Dharma are fewer,
the stick of Ajñātakauṇḍinya must be taken;
if even one stick is in excess, then that legal case is settled, namely, by means of the Dharma.
Thus, when that legal case has been settled, if anyone should deny it, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.

Likewise, if even a single illegal voting-stick (*śalākā*) is in excess, that legal case is nonetheless settled—namely, by means of illegality. When that legal case has been settled in this way, if anyone should deny it, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.

Thus, there is the settling of a legal dispute (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*) by means of the taking of voting sticks according to the majority (*yadbhūyaiṣīka-śalākā-grahaṇa*); in this way, for certain legal disputes, there is taming (*dama*), pacification (*śama*), and complete subsiding (*vyupaśama*), namely, through the settling of disputes by means of the taking of voting sticks according to the majority.

The legal questions arising from *vivāda* (dispute) and *anavavāda* (reproach) can be settled in two and three ways, respectively. Regarding the *smṛtivinaya*, the *Bhikṣu-vibhaṅga* states: "O monks, a legal question concerning dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*) is to be subdued, pacified, and fully settled by means of two methods for settling legal questions:
by means of face-to-face settlement (*saṃmukhavinaya*) and by means of the taking of voting sticks according to the majority (*yadbhūyaiṣīkaśalākāgrahaṇa*)."
Monks, a legal issue concerning lack of instruction is to be subdued, settled, and pacified by three methods for settling legal issues.
By which three?
By the presence before the assembly (saṃmukha-vinaya), by the settlement through mindfulness (smṛti-vinaya), and by the settlement for one who is no longer deluded (amūḍha-vinaya).
And how, monks, does the settlement of a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) occur through the *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence of)?

And how, furthermore, does there come to be the taming, the pacification, and the complete subsiding of certain legal issues—namely, through the settlement of legal issues by means of the *saṃmukhavinaya*?
As before, beginning with one who stands on firm ground, up to the elder (*sthavira*).
For in this way, monks, there is the settlement of a legal dispute through face-to-face resolution;

and thus, for each of the methods of settling legal disputes, there is taming, calming, and complete pacification— namely, by means of the settlement of legal disputes through face-to-face resolution.
And how, monks, does the settlement of a legal dispute through the *smṛtivinaya* (settlement by recollection) come about?

And furthermore, how is it that among these methods for settling legal disputes there is taming, calming, and complete pacification—namely, through the settlement of a legal dispute by means of the *smṛtivinaya*?
It was, for instance, when the venerable Dravya Mallaputra was falsely accused by the nun Mitrā.
Monks, they reprove him for that matter;
being reproved for that matter, he feels ashamed.
The monks report this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, grant the *smṛtivinaya* for the Malla-son regarding the matter. Furthermore, in such cases of this kind, it should be granted in this manner:
having prepared the seating and having struck the gong, and having questioned the monks by means of a formal inquiry, when the entire Saṃgha has assembled and is seated together... (Adhik-v 96)
Having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, crouching down, and joining his palms, Dravya Mallaputra should say this:
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen:
I, Dravya Mallaputra, have been falsely accused by the nun Mitrā."
"Monks, they accuse me on that account; being accused on that account, I request the *smṛtivinaya* from the Saṅgha.
May the venerable Saṅgha, out of compassion, grant me, Dravya Mallaputra, the *smṛtivinaya*."
Thus a second time, and likewise a third time;
thereafter, one monk should make a formal motion (*jñapti*) and perform the ritual act (*karman*):
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen."
This Dravya Mallaputra has been falsely accused by the nun Mitrā;
the monks are now reproving him on account of that matter.
Thus, being accused on account of that matter, he requests the Saṃgha for the *smṛtivinaya* (verdict based on memory).
If it seems the proper time has come for the Saṃgha, and if the Saṃgha should grant permission, let the Saṃgha grant the *smṛtivinaya* to Dravya Mallaputra—this is the motion (*jñapti*).
The formal act (*karman*) should then be performed.
"Listen, venerable Saṃgha:
this Dravya Mallaputra has been falsely accused by the nun Mitrayā;
yet the monks are accusing him on account of that very matter."
Thus, being accused on account of that matter, Dravya Mallaputra requests the *smṛtivinaya* (settlement by recollection) from the Saṃgha.
Therefore, the Saṃgha grants the *smṛtivinaya* to Dravya Mallaputra.
Those venerable ones who consent to granting the *smṛtivinaya* to Dravya Mallaputra should remain silent; those who do not consent, [should speak].
May it be spoken; this is the first formal proclamation (*karmavācanā*);
in this same way, the second and third formal proclamations are to be performed;
the Saṃgha has granted the *smṛtivinaya* for the substance belonging to Mallaputra.
"It has been patiently accepted and authorized by the Saṃgha because of its silence;
thus do I understand this.
[This constitutes] three forms of *smṛtivinaya* that are not legally valid.
There are three unrighteous grants of *smṛtivinaya* and three righteous ones.
What are the three unrighteous grants of *smṛtivinaya*?
For example, suppose a monk has committed an offense involving defeat (*pārājika*).
When the monks reprove him for that matter, and being reproved for that matter, he requests from the Saṃgha a verdict of restoration based on mindfulness (*smṛtivinaya*).
The Saṃgha should grant him a *smṛtivinaya*;
[if it does not do so,] the granting of the *smṛtivinaya* is contrary to the Dharma.
For what reason?
He is deserving of expulsion;
for instance, when a monk has fallen into an offense that is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, a *pāyattika*, a *pratideśanīya*, or a *duṣkṛta*,
and the monks reprove him on account of that very matter.
Being accused on account of that matter, he requests the *smṛtivinaya* from the Saṃgha;
the Saṃgha grants him the *smṛtivinaya*,
which is an unrighteous granting of the *smṛtivinaya*.
For what reason? Because he is worthy of instruction;

for instance, by that monk Sekata—who was naked, insane, deranged in mind, and overwhelmed by painful sensations—much that was unbecoming of a śramaṇa and contrary to the Dharma was practiced, spoken, and attempted.
Saliva flowed, the eyes were wide open, and the face was distorted.
While he was not asleep, it was thought that he was asleep;
while he had not spoken by others, it was thought that he had spoken;
and at another time, he regained his own mind.
Monks, they charge him with that matter;
being charged with that matter, he requests the *smṛtivinaya* from the Saṃgha;
the Saṃgha grants the *smṛtivinaya*.
The granting of a formal act of memory (smṛti-vinaya) for one who is unrighteous;
for what reason?
Because he is one who deserves the formal act for one who is not deluded (amūḍha-vinaya).
It is as follows: a monk who is factually guilty of an offense denies it in the midst of the Saṃgha;
having denied it, he admits it; and having admitted it, he denies it once again.
"Monks, they grant him a *smṛtivinaya* (settlement based on memory),
which is an unrighteous granting of *smṛtivinaya*. Why is that?"
"He is worthy of the *tatsvabhāvaiṣīya*";
thus, these three are the legal applications of *smṛtivinaya*.
These are the three forms of *smṛtivinaya* that are in accordance with the Dharma.
What are the three legal grants of mindfulness and discipline (*smṛti-vinaya-dāna*)? They are as follows:
for instance, Dravya Mallaputra was falsely accused by the nun Mitrā;
the monks then reproached him on account of that matter.
Being exhorted by that matter, he requests the *smṛtivinaya* from the Saṃgha;
the Saṃgha grants him the *smṛtivinaya*;
this is a legal granting of the *smṛtivinaya*.

For example, suppose a monk has committed one particular offense, yet the monks accuse him of another matter; while being accused on that other matter, he requests the *smṛtivinaya* (settlement based on mindfulness) from the Saṃgha.
The Saṃgha grants him a *smṛtivinaya*;
it is a righteous granting of *smṛtivinaya*,
as when a monk has fallen into an offense.
She has confessed that matter before that monk, or it has been remedied;
yet the monks reprove him for that very matter, and being reproved for that matter, he requests the *smṛtivinaya* from the Saṃgha.
The Saṃgha grants him a *smṛtivinaya* (settlement based on mindfulness),
which is a legal grant of *smṛtivinaya*;
thus, these are the three legal grants of *smṛtivinaya*.
For in this way, monks, there is the settling of a legal dispute through the *smṛtivinaya* (settlement by recollection);
in this way, for some disputes here, there is taming, calming, and complete pacification, namely, by means of the settling of disputes through *smṛtivinaya*.
[Next is] the *amūḍhavinaya* (settlement by one not being of unsound mind).
And how, monks, is there the settlement of a legal dispute through the *amūḍhavinaya* (the verdict of past insanity)?
And furthermore, how is it that for some legal disputes here, there is taming, pacification, and complete subsiding—namely, by means of the settlement of a legal dispute through the *amūḍhavinaya*?

It is as follows: suppose a certain monk, being naked, insane, deranged in mind, overwhelmed by painful sensations, has acted, spoken, and exerted himself in many ways that are unbecoming of a recluse and contrary to the Dharma.
Saliva flowed, his eyes rolled back, and his face was disfigured.
While he was not asleep, it was thought that he was asleep;
while he had not spoken by others, it was thought that he had spoken;
and at another time, he regained his own mind.
Monks, they reproved him for that matter; being reproved for that matter, he requested the *amūḍhavinaya* (verdict of no-longer-deluded) from the Saṃgha;
the monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"O monks,
grant the *amūḍhavinaya* (the verdict of one no longer insane) to the monk Sekata."
Or whoever else is of such a kind, it should be given in this manner:
having prepared the seating for the bedding, having struck the gong, and having questioned [the candidate] through a formal inquiry, when the entire Saṃgha is seated and assembled,
a monk who has received the *sekha* (initiation) should arrange his upper robe over one shoulder and perform the proper salutation according to seniority.
Having performed this, one should stand in the *utkuṭuka* posture and speak as follows:

"May the venerable Saṃgha listen: by me, a monk who was a *sekata*, naked, insane, deranged, overwhelmed by painful sensations, much that was unbecoming of a Śramaṇa and improper has been done; [much] has been spoken; saliva has been spat."
His eyes rolled about, his face was distorted,
and though he was not asleep, he was thought to be sleeping.
What was not spoken by others was thought by me to have been spoken; and by that, at another time, I regained my own mind.
Monks, they reproach me on account of that matter.
Thus, being accused on account of that matter, I request the Saṃgha for the *amūḍhavinaya* (verdict of one not insane).
May the venerable Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me, the monk Sekata, the *amūḍhavinaya*.
Thus a second time, and thus a third time.
Thereafter, one monk shall make a formal motion (*jñapti*) and the ritual act (*karman*) should be performed:
"Listen, venerable Saṃgha!

This monk Sekata, being naked, insane, deranged in mind, and overwhelmed by painful sensations, has acted, spoken, and exerted himself in many ways that are unbecoming of a śramaṇa and contrary to the Dharma."
Saliva flowed, the eyes rolled back, and the face was distorted.
While he was not asleep, it was thought that he was asleep;
while he had not spoken by others, it was thought that he had spoken;
and by this other means, his own mind was regained.
Monks, they reprove him for that matter;
being reproved for that matter, he requests from the Saṅgha the *amūḍhavinaya* (verdict of past insanity).
If it seems the right time to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha, if it approves, grant the *amūḍhavinaya* to the monk Sekata. This is the motion (*jñapti*).
An action must be performed.
Listen, venerable Saṃgha:
by this monk Sekata, who was naked, insane, deranged in mind, and overwhelmed by painful sensations, much that is unbecoming of a śramaṇa and contrary to the Dharma has been practiced.
He spoke with great effort,
saliva was discharged, and his eyes rolled back.
And his face was disfigured;
though he was not asleep, he was thought to be asleep,
and though he had not spoken by others, he was thought to have spoken.
And at another time, he regained his own mind;
monks then accused him on account of that matter,
and being thus accused on account of that matter, he requested the *amūḍhavinaya* (verdict of past insanity) from the Saṅgha.
Therefore, the Saṃgha grants the *amūḍhavinaya* (verdict of past insanity) to the monk Sekata;
those venerable ones who consent to granting the *amūḍhavinaya* to the monk Sekata should remain silent.
If it is not approved, let them speak; this is the first formal proclamation (*karmavācanā*); in this same manner, the second and third formal proclamations are to be performed.
The Saṃgha has granted the *amūḍhavinaya* (verdict of past insanity) to the monk Sekata;
it is accepted and authorized by the Saṃgha since there is silence; thus do I understand this. (Adhik-v 100)

There are two forms of *amūḍhavinaya* (verdict of one not being deluded), one of which is non-legal and one of which is legal: one is an illegitimate bestowal of *amūḍhavinaya*, and one is a legitimate [bestowal].
What is the one that is contrary to the Dharma?

It is when a monk who is not insane claims, "I am insane," or one whose mind is not deranged claims, "My mind is deranged"; yet the Saṃgha grants him the *amūḍhavinaya* (the verdict of past insanity).
The granting of the *amūḍhavinaya* to one who is unrighteous;
this is one unrighteous [procedure].
What is the righteous? It is as follows:
a certain newly ordained monk—naked, insane, deranged, overwhelmed by painful sensations—behaved, spoke, and exerted himself in many ways unbecoming of a śramaṇa and contrary to the Dharma;
he even spat out saliva.
His eyes rolled back, his face was distorted, and though he was not asleep, he was thought to be sleeping.
He thought, "I have been addressed by others when I was not actually addressed";
and by that other occasion, he regained his composure.
Monks, they then reproved him on account of that matter.
Thus, being reproved on account of that matter, he requests the *amūḍhavinaya* (verdict of past insanity) from the Saṃgha;
the Saṃgha grants him the *amūḍhavinaya*;
this is a legal granting of the *amūḍhavinaya*.
This is one lawful method;
for in this way, monks, the resolution of disputes through the "decision of the unconfused" becomes a means of settling legal cases;
and furthermore, in this way, there is the taming, the calming, and the complete pacification of certain legal cases here.
Monks, a legal question arising from non-instruction (*anavavādādhikaraṇa*) should be subdued, pacified, and thoroughly settled by these three methods for settling legal questions, namely:
face-to-face resolution (*saṃmukhavinaya*), resolution through mindfulness (*smṛtivinaya*), and resolution for one who is no longer deluded (*amūḍhavinaya*).
A legal question arising from an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*) may be settled in four ways. [The first is] the formal admission of the charge (*pratijñākāraka*).
Monks, a legal issue concerning an offense (āpatty-adhikaraṇa) must be subdued, settled, and pacified by means of four methods for settling legal issues.
Which four?

By means of acting upon a formal admission (pratijñā-kāraka), by means of resolution in the presence of the parties (saṃmukha-vinaya), by means of investigating the nature of the matter (tatsvabhāva-eṣīya), and by means of the "spreading of grass" (tṛṇa-prastāraka).
And how, monks, is there a settlement of a legal dispute (*adhikaraṇa*) by means of a formal admission (*pratijñākāraka*)?

And furthermore, how is it that for some disputes here, there is taming, appeasement, and complete subsiding—namely, by means of the settlement of a legal dispute through a formal admission? It is as follows: a monk has committed an offense (*āpatti*). (Adhik-v 101)

Whether urged by that matter or not urged, whether reminded or not reminded, he stands before a monk and speaks thus: "Pay attention, venerable sir! I, named so-and-so, have fallen into such an offense; I confess it and disclose it in the presence of the venerable one."
"Having confessed and revealed it to me, there will be comfort for me, not by failing to confess and reveal it.
Then he should say, "Do you see the offense?
and the other should also say, "I see it."
The former should say, "Will you undertake restraint for the future? and the latter should say, "I will undertake it. This is the formal declaration (*pratijñā*).

There are ten ways of making a formal proposition (*pratijñākāraka*) that are respectively illegal and legal: ten illegal propositions (*daśādhārmikāṇi pratijñādānāni*) and ten legal ones (*daśa dhārmikāṇi*).
What are the ten unrighteous acts?
For example, when a monk has committed an offense involving defeat (pārājika) yet claims, "I have not committed it," the Saṃgha compels him to admit his claim.
An illegal formal admission:

one who has fallen into an offense that is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, a *pāyattika*, a *pratideśanika*, or a *duṣkṛta*, yet claims "I have not fallen into it," and the Saṃgha causes him to make a formal admission.
An unjust formal admission:
for example, when a monk who has not committed an offense involving defeat (pārājika) admits, "I have committed it," and the Saṃgha causes him to make that admission.
An illegal formal admission:
one who has not committed an offense that is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, a *pāyattika*, a *pratideśanika*, or a *duṣkṛta*, yet admits "I have committed it," and the Saṃgha causes him to make that admission.
There is the making of an unrighteous promise;
these are the ten unrighteous promises. What are the ten righteous promises?
It is as follows: when a monk has committed an offense involving defeat (*pārājika*) and confesses, "I have committed it," the Saṃgha causes him to make a formal confession.
The formal undertaking of a legal claim is as follows:

when one has committed an offense that is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, a *pāyattika*, a *pratideśanika*, or a *duṣkṛta*, and he acknowledges, "I have committed it," the Saṃgha causes him to undertake that formal claim.
A formal admission that is in accordance with the Dharma:
for example, when a monk who has not committed a *pārājika* offense declares, "I have not committed one," and the Saṃgha causes him to make that admission,
it is a formal admission that is in accordance with the Dharma.

If one confesses, "I have not committed an offense that is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, a *pāyattika*, a *pratideśanika*, or a *duṣkṛta*," the Saṃgha causes him to make this confession; this is a lawful acceptance of a confession. These are the ten lawful acceptances of a confession.

(Adhik-v 102) For in this way, monks, there is the settling of a legal dispute through the method of self-accusation (*pratijñākāraka*); thus, for some disputes here, there is taming, pacification, and complete subsiding, namely, by means of the settling of disputes through self-accusation.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery. At that time, the Venerable Kāla Mṛgāraputra was staying at Vaiśālī, in the Gabled Hall on the bank of the Markaṭahrada. The Buddha absolved the monk Kāla Mṛgāraputra of a false accusation.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery; at that time, the Venerable Kāla Mṛgāraputra was staying at Vaiśālī, in the Gabled Hall on the bank of the Markaṭahrada.
Having come upon him, the Licchavis of Vaiśālī performed services for the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha to an extraordinary degree.
The monks of Vaiśālī reflected:
"The venerable Kāla Mṛgāraputra was born elsewhere."
He grew up in that very place, having been born in Śrāvastī;
and the Licchavis of Vaiśālī were exceedingly devoted to him.

"Therefore, a formal act of suspension (*utkṣepaṇīya-karman*) should be performed against him, so that the Licchavis of Vaiśālī will no longer manifest their faith toward us. Thus, they became intent on watching for his downfall.
Now, a certain householder invited the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, to a bath in a steam-heated room (*jentāka*).
The monks, having placed their robes in a thicket, began to bathe.
But the venerable Kāla, son of Mṛgāra, being fully aware, set aside his robes in a secluded spot and began to bathe;
another monk also set aside his robes in that very same place.
Then the venerable Kāla, son of Mṛgāra, having bathed and thinking, "These are my own robes," put on the robes belonging to that other monk and departed.
When that monk arose, he did not see his own robes;
he began to ask the monks: "Venerable sirs," he said.
"By whom have my robes been stolen?
Then, he heard that the venerable Kāla Mṛgāraputra’s co-resident was staying in that very place.
He said: "Venerable one, the robes were placed in this spot by the preceptor."
"By that reversal, they would have been led away.
"I shall go now and see the preceptor.
He went into the presence of the preceptor and said:
"Upādhyāya, have you brought back the robes belonging to you? He replied:
"Son, these belong to me; to whom else could they belong?
Preceptor, a certain monk has left his robes in that very place."
He reproached him, saying:
"Son, if it is so, bring them; I wish to see those robes."
Having taken them, he returned and said,
"Preceptor, do you recognize these robes?"
He recognized them and said,
"Son, I brought these by mistake; take these back to that monk."
Having taken them, he went to that monk and said,
"Venerable sir, these robes have been taken by your preceptor by mistake.
He replied:
Having committed an offense involving defeat (*pārājika*), he took those [goods] with a thieving mind;
then, those monks, seeking an opportunity against him, performed an act of suspension (*utkṣepaṇīya-karman*) by force, without having first accused or reminded him.
The Venerable Kāla, son of Mṛgāra, reflected:
"O brahmins and householders, people are won over through suffering and not through happiness;
if I remain here, the Licchavis of Vaiśālī will certainly manifest faith toward us."
Thinking, "In any case, I shall go to Śrāvastī itself," he did not look back at the Licchavis of Vaiśālī, but taking his bowl and robe, set out on a walking tour toward Śrāvastī.
Traveling by stages, he arrived at Śrāvastī; there he was seen by the monks, who said to him:
"Welcome, welcome, venerable Kāla! We are pleased by the sight of you, but not by your arrival.
For what reason?

Because now that you have come, the Licchavis of Vaiśālī—who are devoted to the Buddha, devoted to the Dharma, and devoted to the Saṅgha—perform exceedingly great services toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha."

The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One;

Then the Blessed One reinstated Dharmika;
remorse arose among the people of Vaiśālī.
"It was not well done by us that we forcibly performed the *utkṣepaṇīya* (suspension) rite against the blameless and harmless monk Kāla.
Taking up their bowls and robes, they set out on a journey toward Śrāvastī. On the way, they saw the monk and said to him:
"From where have you come, venerable sir?
"From Śrāvastī.
"Have you seen Kāla Mṛgāraputra?"
It has been seen. What of it?
We have performed a formal act of suspension against him by force—without having accused or reminded him—though he was blameless and had done us no harm; and now he has been reinstated.
By whom? By the Blessed One.
Regarding this, some say: "It has not been revoked, it has been revoked at a distance;
because we performed the act of suspension against him while he was not present before us, his revocation is not proper."
Thus it is said; others, however, say this:
"The Blessed One is the Lord of Dharma; the Sugata is the Lord of Dharma."
Having completed their robes and bowls, they arrived in due course at Śrāvastī; having put away their robes and bowls and washed their feet, they approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the monks of Vaiśālī said this to the Blessed One:

"Venerable Sir, we—fools, deluded, unskilled, and inexperienced—performed a formal act of suspension against Kāla, the son of Mṛgāra, who was blameless and had done us no harm, without having accused him or reminded him of his offense.
Having become filled with remorse, we have come here to ask Kāla, the son of Mṛgāra, for forgiveness."
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, that legal case has been settled by the Tathāgata in accordance with the Dharma.
[They replied: "Venerable Sir, we heard from the mouth of a monk on the way here that the Blessed One had settled it in accordance with the Dharma."
However, some among us say this: "It was not expelled, it was expelled from afar, because we were not present there face-to-face."
But others say this:
"The Blessed One is the Lord of Dharma; the Sugata is the Lord of Dharma. For whomsoever [a charge] has been raised, it is truly raised"—thus are the various forms of accusation.
The Blessed One reflected:
"Alas, my disciples desire to settle each dispute as it arises—namely, by means of the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction.
Having understood this, he addressed the monks:
Monks, how does the settlement of legal issues (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*) by means of face-to-face resolution (*saṃmukha-vinaya*) come about?

And furthermore, how is it that for some legal issues here, there is taming (*dama*), pacification (*śama*), and complete subsiding (*vyupaśama*)—namely, through the settlement of legal issues by means of face-to-face resolution? Here, monks, [first: 1)

6) many persons reprove one person according to the Dharma and the Vinaya, in the presence [of the accused], with four eyes.

1) Many individuals accuse two [individuals] before the Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, face-to-face and with the fourfold presence; 2) Two [individuals] accuse many individuals before the Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, face-to-face and with the fourfold presence; 3) Many individuals accuse the Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, face-to-face and with the fourfold presence; 4) The Saṃgha accuses an individual in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, face-to-face and with the fourfold presence; 5) The Saṃgha accuses two [individuals] before the Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, face-to-face and with the fourfold presence; 6) The Saṃgha accuses many individuals before the Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, face-to-face and with the fourfold presence.

sixteen dharmic [applications].

In this way, monks, there is the settlement of a legal question through the *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence of the parties);

and furthermore, in this manner, for certain legal questions, there is taming, pacification, and complete subsiding, namely, through the settlement of legal questions by means of the *saṃmukhavinaya*.
The settlement of legal questions by the *sadbhāvaiṣīya* method:
And how, monks, is there a settlement of a legal dispute by means of investigating its own nature?

And furthermore, how is it that for some legal disputes here, there is taming, pacification, and complete subsiding— namely, by means of the settlement of legal disputes through investigating its own nature?
In this case, the monk Hastaka denies an offense in the midst of the Saṃgha;
having denied it, he admits it; having admitted it, he again denies it.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One;
the Blessed One said:

"Monks, you should grant the *tatsvabhāviṣīya* (the forfeiture of the object itself) to the monk Hastaka, or to any other who is of a similar nature; and furthermore, it should be granted in this manner."

Having prepared the seats and bedding, struck the gong, and exhorted the monks by means of a formal inquiry, when the entire Saṃgha has sat down and assembled, the monk Hastaka should arrange his upper robe over one shoulder, perform the proper salutation according to seniority, and standing in a squatting position, speak as follows:
Venerable sirs, let the Saṃgha listen: by me, the monk Hastaka, an offense was acknowledged in the midst of the Saṃgha; having acknowledged it, it was confessed.
Having made this promise, I was again treated with contempt;
therefore, I request from the Saṅgha a *tatsvabhāvaiṣīya* [inquiry into the nature of the offense].
May the venerable Saṅgha grant me, the monk Hastaka, a *tatsvabhāvaiṣīya*, out of compassion.
Thus a second time, and thus a third time;
thereafter, after one monk has made the formal motion (*jñapti*), the ritual act (*karman*) should be performed:
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen!..."
This monk Hastaka denies his offense in the midst of the Saṃgha; having denied it, he admits it; having admitted it, he denies it again.
This monk Hastaka requests from the Saṃgha a *tatsvabhāvaiṣīya* (an inquiry into his own nature).

If it seems the proper time to the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha grant its permission that the Saṃgha shall grant the *tatsvabhāvaiṣīya* (investigation of his own nature) to the monk Hastaka; this is the motion (*jñapti*).
The formal act (*karma*) must be performed:
"Let the venerable Saṃgha listen.
This very monk Hastaka denies his offense in the midst of the Saṃgha;
having denied it, he admits it; and having admitted it, he denies it once again.
Therefore, the Saṃgha grants the *tatsvabhāvaiṣīya* (inquiry into the nature of the offense) to the monk Hastaka.
Those venerable ones who consent to granting the *tatsvabhāvaiṣīya* to the monk Hastaka should remain silent;
those who do not consent should speak.
This is the first formal proclamation (*karmavācanā*); in this same manner, the second and third formal proclamations are to be performed.
The Saṃgha has granted the *tatsvabhāvaiṣīya* [penance] to the monk Hastaka.
The Saṃgha has consented and authorized this, since it is silent;
thus do I hold it.
I shall now prescribe the rules of proper conduct for a monk to whom a *tatsvabhāvaiṣīya* (an investigation into his own nature) has been granted.

A monk who has been granted the *tatsvabhāvaiṣīya* penance must not grant the going-forth, must not confer full ordination, must not give dependence, must not have a novice attend upon him, must not perform formal acts (*karman*),
must not be appointed as the performer of formal acts,
and must not instruct the nuns.
A nun must not be appointed as an instructor;

nor should nuns be instructed by one who has been previously appointed; nor should this [nun] reprove or remind a monk regarding a failure in morality, a failure in view, a failure in conduct, or a failure in livelihood.
Instruction should not be given by him;
nor [should it be given] during the Poṣadha ceremony, nor during the Pravāraṇā ceremony.

The Vinaya is not to be relinquished during a formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya*) or a motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha*), nor within the midst of the Saṃgha, provided there are other individuals present who are experts in the Vinaya.

Furthermore, a monk to whom a *tatsvabhāvaiṣīya* (penance for seeking the nature of his offense) has been assigned must not fail to undertake and abide by the rules of customary conduct as they have been prescribed.
One becomes guilty of an offense by giving one such *tatsvabhāvaiṣīya* gift that is contrary to the Dharma and one that is in accordance with the Dharma.
What is the one that is contrary to the Dharma?
It is as follows: the monk Hastaka confesses an offense in the midst of the Saṃgha, but having confessed it, he denies it; having denied it, he confesses it again.
The Saṃgha then grants him a *svabhāvaiṣīya* (an inquiry into his own nature); that granting of a *svabhāvaiṣīya* is contrary to the Dharma.
This is one case that is contrary to the Dharma.
What is the one case that is in accordance with the Dharma? It is as follows:
the monk Hastaka denies an offense in the midst of the Saṃgha; having denied it, he admits it; having admitted it, he denies it again. Regarding him, the Saṃgha—
He grants a *tatsvabhāvaiṣīya* (a formal inquiry regarding the nature of the offense);
this gift of a *tatsvabhāvaiṣīya* is in accordance with the Dharma;
this is the first [type] that is in accordance with the Dharma.

For in this way, monks, there is the settlement of a legal question through the investigation of its intrinsic nature (*tatsvabhāvaiṣīya*); and furthermore, in this manner, for each individual legal question, there is taming, pacification, and complete subsiding—namely, by means of the settlement of legal questions through the investigation of its intrinsic nature.
The settlement of legal questions by the *tṛṇaprastāraka* (spreading of grass) method.
And how, monks, does the settlement of legal disputes by means of the "covering over with grass" (tṛṇaprastāraka) come about?

And how, furthermore, does there occur here for some legal disputes both subduing, appeasement, and complete cessation—namely, by means of the settlement of legal disputes through the "covering over with grass"?
It is as follows: when monks dwell having fallen into quarrels, having become contentious, being divided, having entered into disputes, and being established in opposing factions.

In one faction, there is a monk who is an elder, or one of the elders; well-known, or one of those who are well-known; preeminent, or one of those who are preeminent. Having approached his own faction, he should speak as follows:
"Venerable sirs, for us it is a loss, not a gain; it is ill-acquired, not well-acquired."
We, who have gone forth in this well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, dwell having become quarrelsome, contentious, disputatious, and fallen into strife;
and as for the offense I have committed in this matter, O Venerable Ones, and that which you have committed—
setting aside a grave offense or one involving a layperson— [I confess it].
"I am willing, by means of my own duty, to confess, reveal, and not conceal [this offense] before you and those venerable ones.
If even a single monk from that monk's own faction does not reject or oppose what has been said,

then that monk, having approached the other faction, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, having performed the proper salutation according to seniority, and having crouched down, should speak as follows:

"Venerable sirs, it is a loss for us, not a gain; it is ill-gained by us, not well-gained, that we, having gone forth in this well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, dwell engaged in quarreling, brawling, contending, and falling into disputes.
And as for the offense I have incurred in this matter, and those which you venerable sirs have incurred—"

"Setting aside a grave offense or one for which a householder is the refuge, I am willing— out of my own duty— to confess, reveal, and not conceal [this offense] before those venerable ones, you. In the second case, a monk who is an elder, or one among the elders, who is well-known, or one among the well-known, who is prominent, or one among the prominent, having approached his own faction, should say this:

Venerable sirs, it is a loss for us and for them, not a gain; it is ill-gained, not well-gained, that we, having gone forth in this well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, dwell having given rise to quarrels, having given rise to strife, being contentious and fallen into dispute.
And as for the offense I have incurred, venerable sirs, in this matter, and the one you have incurred—
"Setting aside a grave offense or one for which a householder is the refuge,
I am able, by means of my own effort, to confess, reveal, and not conceal [my fault] before you, venerable sirs.
If even a single monk from that monk's own faction speaks thus:

He neither opposes nor protests. Then that monk, having approached the second faction, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, having performed the proper salutation according to seniority, and having stood in a squatting position, should speak as follows:
"Venerable sirs, it is a loss for us, not a gain; it is ill-gotten for us, not well-gotten."

We, who have gone forth in this well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya, dwell having fallen into quarreling, brawling, contention, and dispute; and whatever offense I have incurred in this matter, and whatever those venerable ones have incurred— setting aside a grave offense or one involving a layperson— [we acknowledge it].
"I am able, by means of my own duty, to confess, reveal, and not conceal [my faults] in the presence of those venerable ones,
you. When one side causes a hair to fall on the second side, brings about an exit, and brings about a reconciliation, or when the second side does so toward the first,
and they do not proceed by mutually proclaiming their offenses—
In this way, that legal case is settled by means of the settlement of disputes known as "spreading the grass" (*tṛṇaprastāraka*);
for such, monks, is the settlement of disputes by spreading the grass.

It happens thus: furthermore, for certain legal cases here, there is subduing, calming, and complete pacification—namely, by means of the *tṛṇaprastāraka* (covering with grass) method of settling disputes.

Monks, a legal case concerning an offense must be subdued, calmed, and completely pacified by these four methods for settling disputes, namely: by means of the *pratijñākāraka* (acting according to confession), the *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence of the parties), the *tatsvabhāvaiṣīya* (investigation into the nature of the act), and the *tṛṇaprastāraka*.
Monks, a legal case concerning duties must be settled by the entire Saṅgha.
In whatever residence there dwells only one monk, there is no quarrel, strife, contention, or dispute;
and in whatever [residence] there are two, there too there is no quarrel, strife, contention, or dispute.
Where there are three, even there there is no quarreling, brawling, strife, or dispute;
but where four monks reside, or more than that, there is quarreling, brawling, strife, and dispute.
Just so, monks...
One is like Brahmā; two are like Śakra;
three are like the king; beyond that is tumultuous noise.
Therefore, monks, I authorize this: to whoever memorizes even a single four-line stanza, the property belonging to the Dharma must be given to him, and he too may make use of it.
No regret should be felt in this matter.
The section on the subject of legal cases (*adhikaraṇavastu*) is concluded.
